characters: Ama: a girl of about five, braided hair with yellow ribbons, a blue dress, bare feet or simple sandals.
Pepe: a small brown goat with one white spot on his nose.
Grandpa Yaw: a kind elderly man with a white beard and a walking stick.
The hen: a speckled hen with four chicks.

narrationPlan.voice: Warm female storyteller, Ghanaian English (en-GH), unhurried.
narrationPlan.pace: Slow (about 100 words per minute) for the youngest listeners.
notes: Distinct but gentle voices for the hen and Grandpa Yaw.
Leave about 0.6 s of silence between pages.
Goat bleats performed by the narrator, not sound-effect files, so timing stays exact.

ama-lost-little-goat.music: Optional soft village morning ambience (kalimba and light percussion). Not created; needs a verified licence before use.
culturalNotes: Ama and Yaw are Akan day names (born on Saturday / Thursday). A Ghanaian reviewer should confirm they are used naturally.
Free-roaming goats tied with rope near a family compound are common in villages.
reviewQuestions: Is "Grandpa Yaw" a natural form of address for this setting?
Is the level right for Nursery 2 to KG 1 listeners (sentence length, vocabulary)?

pages.brief: Warm morning light. Ama hugging Pepe in front of a family compound. The white spot on Pepe’s nose clearly visible.

characters: Efua: a girl of thirteen, JHS uniform, practical and thoughtful.
Nana Ama: her grandmother, patient and wise.
Kwabena: her classmate, confident and always looking for shortcuts.
Auntie Dede: a market trader who gives Efua advice.

narrationPlan.voice: Natural, mature storyteller, Ghanaian English. Subtle character differences, no caricature.
narrationPlan.pace: Medium (about 140 words per minute).
notes: Numbers must be spoken clearly and consistently with the text (check twelve, eight, forty, twenty, twenty-five, eleven, nine, thirteen).
Names go through the pronunciation dictionary; all entries are still awaiting native-speaker review.

efuas-honest-business.music: No background music: text-first reading experience for older learners. Optional soft ambience toggle only.
culturalNotes: Groundnut cakes (nkate cake and similar sweets) are a familiar local treat; a reviewer should confirm the recipe description and the realism of prices in cedis for the intended year.
The names are Akan day names (Efua, Kwabena, Ama); Dede’s origin must be confirmed.
reviewQuestions: Are the prices realistic for the intended region and year? (Amounts are illustrative.)
Does the dilemma suit JHS and avoid moralising?
Is the groundnut-cake recipe description (roasted groundnuts and sugar) right for what learners know as groundnut cakes?
Is the cost-per-pack arithmetic (65 pesewas, 13 cedis for twenty) consistent everywhere?

pages.brief: Nana Ama and Efua stir a pot of golden sugar and groundnuts together on a charcoal stove, steam rising in the morning light. Must show: the pot of glossy golden groundnuts; Nana’s wooden spoon; steam in the light. Camera: medium two-shot, slightly above the pot. Lighting: warm window light with golden steam.
pages.narration: Warm, unhurried, a smile in the voice. Let "quick hands and patient eyes" sound like a saying Nana Ama repeats.

image.alt: A thirteen-year-old girl stirs a pot beside her grandmother in a warm kitchen, golden groundnuts and sugar glowing in the pot.

pages.brief: Efua, hopeful, looks to her grandmother, who playfully points to an exercise book and pencil on the kitchen table. Must show: blue exercise book with pencil; finished groundnut cakes cooling on a tray. Camera: medium two-shot at table height. Lighting: soft late-morning window light.
pages.narration: Bright and hopeful for the plan; Nana Ama gentle and teasing.

pages.brief: Efua writes neat columns of costs and profit in her exercise book at a small table under a warm lamp. Must show: exercise book with simple handwritten sums (numbers only, no readable words); pencil in hand; lamp glow on her face. Camera: close medium shot over her shoulder showing the page. Lighting: single warm lamp, deep indigo background.
pages.narration: Measured, working-it-out pace; slow and clear on every number (twelve, one, eight, forty).

pages.brief: At the school gate, Efua hands a paper-wrapped pack to a smiling student; a cloth bag of leftover packs sits at her feet. Must show: paper-wrapped packs on a small table; a cloth bag of leftover packs at her feet; two or three students in uniform. Camera: medium shot, Efua at right, queue at left. Lighting: late-afternoon golden light.
pages.narration: Picks up pace for the sales, then slows and dips on "gone a little soft".

pages.brief: Kwabena leans in near the gate, glancing at the bag of soft cakes, while Efua looks uncertain. Must show: the bag of soft cakes; Kwabena’s persuasive grin; Efua’s uncertain look. Camera: medium two-shot, slightly low. Lighting: late-afternoon, shade under the tree.
pages.narration: Kwabena smooth, friendly, reasonable-sounding. Not a villain.

pages.brief: Kwabena smiles confidently and points at the old packs, as if it is the most sensible idea in the world; Efua hesitates. Must show: old packs in the bag; Kwabena’s confident gesture; Efua hesitating. Camera: two-shot, eye level, shallow depth of field. Lighting: soft shade with warm highlights.
pages.narration: Confident, easy. A beat of silence after "fresh today" before the final clause. Efua’s silence lands.

pages.brief: Alone by lamplight, Efua sits still with her exercise book open, thinking hard, a deep blue night sky in the window. Must show: open exercise book with numbers; lamp glow; night sky in the window. Camera: medium shot from the side, lamp as the key light. Lighting: warm lamp, indigo night, gentle moonlight.
pages.narration: Slow, reflective. Let each number breathe. Slow further on "trust" and lower the voice on the last line.

pages.brief: Auntie Dede arranges a pyramid of tomatoes at her stall and speaks kindly to Efua, who listens carefully. Must show: pyramid of tomatoes; Auntie Dede’s red-and-gold head-tie; Efua listening. Camera: medium two-shot with the tomato pyramid in the foreground. Lighting: warm morning light through the cloth awning.
pages.narration: Auntie Dede warm, firm, experienced; a gentle smile in the voice on "garden".

pages.brief: Efua’s hands fill a paper pack with extra groundnut cakes and write the date on a small label; a second bag is marked as half price. Must show: extra groundnuts in the pack; handwritten date on the label (numbers only); a separate bag marked for half price, shown with a simple symbol, no readable words. Camera: close-up on her hands and the packs, her face softly visible. Lighting: warm kitchen light.
pages.narration: Quiet pride, steady pace. Read the label text clearly.

pages.brief: A longer queue of cheerful students at the school gate; Efua serves with a smile. Must show: the long queue; Efua serving; the half-price bag on the table. Camera: wide medium shot, queue leading the eye to Efua. Lighting: golden afternoon.
pages.narration: Even, content, building quietly.

pages.brief: Kwabena, at the front of the queue, sheepishly smiles as Efua holds out a fresh pack of groundnut cakes. Must show: Kwabena sheepish; the pack being held out; the queue behind him. Camera: medium two-shot, warm and friendly. Lighting: golden afternoon, soft rim light.
pages.narration: Kwabena a little sheepish, honest. Efua’s last line dry and warm: she charges him, and it is funny.

pages.brief: Efua writes the date at the top of a fresh page in her exercise book, smiling quietly, a jar of groundnuts beside her. Must show: fresh page; jar of groundnuts; quiet smile. Camera: medium close shot, warm and calm. Lighting: warm lamp, soft indigo night.
pages.narration: Satisfied, understated; slow down on the last sentence and let "honestly" settle.

teacherGuide.overview: Efua starts a small groundnut-cake business and is tempted by a classmate’s shortcuts. The story joins real arithmetic (cost, revenue, profit) to a choice about honesty, and shows that a trustworthy reputation is part of a business’s value.
learningGoals: Work out cost, income and profit from a simple business and check a claim against the numbers.
Explain why trust and honesty matter to customers and to a business over time.
Infer a character’s reasoning and the meaning of a metaphor ("customers are like a garden").
Apply the story to a real choice in the learner’s own life.

subjectLinks.link: Money, cost and profit; checking a claim with calculation.

subjectLinks.link: Reading comprehension, inference, vocabulary, discussion.

beforeReading: Ask: "Have you ever bought something from a school-gate seller? What made you go back, or not?"
Pre-teach: profit, cost, trust. Write "profit = money in − money spent" on the board.
whileReading: After page 3, pause for the profit activity: check every learner can get to eight cedis.
After page 6, ask for predictions before reading on (the prediction activity).
After page 7, let learners check Kwabena’s "twice the profit" claim with Efua’s numbers.
afterReading: Put the events in order, then retell the story in three sentences.
Have learners recalculate with the final recipe: cost 65 pesewas per pack, selling at one cedi.
discussion: Was Kwabena a bad person, or someone giving poor advice? How do you know?
Efua made less profit on some days. What did she gain that the sums alone do not show?
How was selling leftover cakes at half price different from calling them fresh?
What does "Customers are like a garden" mean? Can you think of another comparison?
reflection: Think of a time you were tempted to take a shortcut. What did you do, and what would you do now?
What do people say about you when you are not there? How could you build a reputation you are proud of?
Where in your own life (school, home, a small job, a class project) does honesty cost you something in the short term and pay off later?
Who is your "Auntie Dede", someone whose advice you trust? What makes them trustworthy?

mathsExtension.task: Efua sells all 20 packs at 1 cedi each. Cost 12 cedis. What is the profit?
On Monday she sold 14 packs of the 20 she made. What was her profit?
mathsExtension.answer: 14 − 12 = 2 cedis (the six unsold packs were already paid for).

mathsExtension.task: With fewer groundnuts, 20 packs cost 9 cedis. What is the profit if all 20 sell? How much more than 8 cedis is that?
mathsExtension.answer: 20 − 9 = 11 cedis, which is 3 cedis more. Kwabena promised "twice", which would be 16.

mathsExtension.task: The honest recipe costs 65 pesewas a pack. What do 25 packs cost, and what is the profit if all sell at 1 cedi?
mathsExtension.answer: 25 × 65 = 1,625 pesewas = 16.25 cedis. Profit 25 − 16.25 = 8.75 cedis, more than the original 8 cedis.

mathsExtension.task: Challenge: Efua sells 5 half-price packs (50 pesewas each) and 20 full-price packs a day. Cost: 16.25 cedis for 25 packs. What is the profit?
mathsExtension.answer: Income 20 + 2.50 = 22.50 cedis. Profit 22.50 − 16.25 = 6.25 cedis. Honest half-price selling costs a little, and still earns trust.

support: Use whole-cedi numbers only (pages 3 and 7) and a number line for subtraction.
Read pages aloud in "Listen" mode and discuss with a partner before answering.
stretch: Ask learners to design their own small business and cost it, including how they would handle leftovers honestly.
Compare Kwabena’s claim with Efua’s calculation and write a two-sentence rebuttal.

culturalNotes: The names are Akan day names: Efua (a girl born on Friday), Kwabena (a boy born on Tuesday), Ama (a girl born on Saturday). Dede is used in several Ghanaian communities; a reviewer should confirm its origin before it is described in print.
"Nana" is a respectful title for an elder or grandparent. "Auntie" is a common courtesy title for a woman who is not necessarily a relative.
Groundnut cakes (nkate cake and similar sweets) are a familiar snack. A local reviewer should confirm the recipe description.
localiseThis: Prices are illustrative: check that 12 cedis for 20 packs and a 1 cedi selling price suit your area and year, and adjust the numbers and answers together.
Choose a school uniform colour that matches your school if learners will see illustrations of the gate.

reviewerNotes: Confirm vowel quality and whether the final syllable is stressed.

pronunciation.guidance: Candidate: three soft syllables, "eh-FOO-ah". A two-syllable "EH-fwah" is also heard in English speech.
reviewerNotes: Choose between "eh-FOO-ah" (3 syllables) and "EH-fwah" (2) for the narrator voice.
Supply IPA and mark tone if wanted.
Confirm language of origin and meaning before it appears in teacher notes.

characters: Yaa: a girl of nine, curious and determined, with a notebook.
Kofi: her younger brother, cheerful and casual.
Auntie Akosua and Mr Mensah: helpful neighbours.
The head teacher: encouraging.

narrationPlan.voice: Clear, lively storyteller (en-GH or en-GB); a curious, determined girl’s voice for Yaa without imitating a child.
narrationPlan.pace: Medium (about 120 words per minute).
notes: Say forty-two and six clearly.
Names go through the pronunciation dictionary (unverified).

yaa-and-the-blocked-drain.music: Optional gentle rain ambience on the first pages; off by default. Not created.
culturalNotes: The drain, flooded lane and recycling collection are common in many Ghanaian towns; confirm local recycling practice before the final version (is plastic actually collected locally?).
Names are Akan; pronunciation needs native review.
reviewQuestions: Is the recycling description accurate for most schools (is collection available)?
Is Yaa leading the neighbours (an adult-led community) plausible, or should an adult guide her more explicitly?
Is the safety of children working at a drain addressed (gloves, adult supervision)? Consider adding a line about an adult supervising.

teacherGuide.overview: A girl investigates why the lane floods, counts the rubbish, leads her community to clear the drain and starts a school club that tracks the improvement with numbers. Models the scientific habit of observing, counting and checking.
learningGoals: Explain how a blocked drain causes flooding.
Use counting and subtraction to show a change over time.
Describe one small action that protects the local environment.

beforeReading: Ask: "What happens to rainwater after it falls on our school?"
Look at a photo or drawing of a drain (use a local one).
whileReading: Pause after page 4 and ask learners to explain, in a sentence, why the water was stuck.
After page 5, ask what Yaa should do next.
afterReading: Do a 10-minute rubbish count of a safe area at school and chart it.
Compare with a count a week later.
discussion: Why did Yaa count the rubbish instead of just clearing it?

teacherGuide.overview: Set at the real Ghana Radio Astronomy Observatory at Kuntunse, this story introduces JHS learners to modern cosmology: the expansion of space, galaxies, stellar nucleosynthesis, the observable universe, the three pillars of Big Bang evidence, and the boundary between established evidence and open scientific questions.
learningGoals: Explain why the Big Bang is an expansion of space itself everywhere rather than an explosion from one point into empty space.
Describe key scientific evidence for cosmic expansion: redshift of distant galaxies, the Cosmic Microwave Background, and primordial hydrogen and helium.
Distinguish between the observable universe and the entire universe.
Distinguish well-supported scientific findings from unresolved questions at the frontier of physics.

beforeReading: Ask learners: "When you look at the night sky, how long do you think starlight takes to reach your eyes?"
Locate Kuntunse (near Accra) on a map of Ghana and introduce the 32-metre Ghana Radio Astronomy Observatory.
whileReading: Pause after page 4 to examine the raisin-bread analogy: ask what the dough represents (space) and what the raisins represent (galaxies).
Pause after page 9 to connect redshift and the Cosmic Microwave Background as two independent lines of evidence.

Discuss why saying "we do not know yet" is a strength, not a weakness, in science.
discussion: Where does the raisin-bread analogy work well, and where does it break down? (Unlike a loaf of bread, the universe has no outer crust or kitchen outside it.)
Why do galaxies like the Milky Way not get stretched apart as space expands? (Local gravity binds a galaxy together.)
Why can we only see the observable universe and not beyond it?
reflection: What is one question about space or nature that you would love to investigate as a scientist or engineer?
How does checking evidence help us avoid misunderstandings in everyday life as well as in science?

mathsExtension.task: Light travels about 300,000 km per second. How far does light travel in 10 seconds?
The Kuntunse radio dish has a diameter of 32 metres. What is its radius?

support: Use a lightly inflated balloon with paper stickers (representing galaxies) so learners see the stickers move apart without the stickers themselves growing.
stretch: Write a short paragraph explaining how a scientist uses both optical telescopes and radio telescopes to study the universe.

culturalNotes: Abena (girl born on Tuesday) and Kwame (boy born on Saturday) are Akan day names; Mensah is a common Ghanaian surname.

The Ghana Radio Astronomy Observatory at Kuntunse was converted from a former satellite telecommunications dish and inaugurated in 2017 as part of the African Very Long Baseline Interferometry Network (AVN) and Square Kilometre Array (SKA) partnership.
localiseThis: Connect night-sky observation to clear dry-season evenings in your community and discuss how street lighting affects how many stars we see.

factCheck.claim: The Big Bang was an expansion of space everywhere from an extremely hot, dense state ~13.8 billion years ago, not an explosion from a single point into pre-existing empty space.
factCheck.explanation: General relativity and cosmological observations (Planck collaboration, 2018) show metric expansion of space itself with an age of 13.787 ± 0.020 billion years.
factCheck.reference: NASA Wilkinson Microwave Anisotropy Probe (WMAP) & ESA Planck Mission Cosmology Overview; IAU Office of Astronomy for Education.
factCheck.analogyNote: The rising raisin-bread analogy illustrates uniform expansion between unbound galaxy clusters, but teachers should note that galaxies themselves stay bound by gravity and real space has no external "oven" or boundary.

factCheck.claim: Redshift of distant galaxies, the Cosmic Microwave Background (released ~380,000 years after the Big Bang), and light-element abundances are the primary observational pillars of Big Bang cosmology.
factCheck.explanation: Cosmological redshift stretches photon wavelengths as the scale factor increases; recombination at ~380,000 years released the CMB now observed at 2.725 K.
factCheck.reference: Peebles, P. J. E. (2020), Principles of Physical Cosmology; NASA Goddard Space Flight Center CMB Education Resources.

factCheck.claim: What happened at t = 0 (the Planck epoch) and the exact nature of dark matter and dark energy remain unresolved scientific questions.
factCheck.explanation: Current physics requires a unified theory of quantum gravity to describe t = 0, and dark matter/dark energy remain active areas of empirical investigation.
factCheck.reference: National Academy of Sciences — Science, Evolution, and Creationism / Cosmology FAQ.

factCheck.claim: Cocoa flowers (Theobroma cacao) are primarily pollinated by tiny biting midges (family Ceratopogonidae, especially Forcipomyia species) that breed in moist leaf litter.
factCheck.explanation: Unlike large bees, tiny Ceratopogonid midges are small enough to enter the intricate hood of cocoa flowers and transfer pollen.
factCheck.reference: Cocoa Research Institute of Ghana (CRIG) & FAO Pollination Services for Sustainable Agriculture.

factCheck.claim: Kakum National Park provides habitat for African forest elephants (Loxodonta cyclotis), Diana monkeys (Cercopithecus diana), yellow-casqued hornbills (Ceratogymna elata), and trees such as odum (Milicia excelsa) and wawa (Triplochiton scleroxylon).
factCheck.explanation: All named species are documented native inhabitants of Ghana’s Upper Guinean moist evergreen forest zone at Kakum.
factCheck.reference: Forestry Commission of Ghana (Wildlife Division) — Kakum National Park Biodiversity Records; IUCN Red List.

factCheck.claim: Straw-coloured fruit bats (Eidolon helvum) disperse seeds across West African forests and savannahs, and fungi, termites, millipedes and bacteria decompose dead wood into soil nutrients.
factCheck.explanation: Eidolon helvum is a keystone seed disperser for reforestation in Ghana; saprotrophic fungi and detritivores mineralise organic matter.
factCheck.reference: University of Ghana Department of Animal Biology and Conservation Science; UNESCO MAB Biosphere Reserve Studies.

teacherGuide.overview: Set at a science museum in Accra, this story helps Primary 6 and JHS 1 learners understand inherited variation, fossils, adaptation, and natural selection, while addressing three widespread misconceptions: teleological individual change ("changing because you need to"), the "humans came from today’s monkeys" myth, and the everyday vs scientific meaning of "theory".
learningGoals: Explain how natural selection acts on inherited variation over many generations.
Clarify why individual organisms do not evolve in their own lifetime simply by wishing or needing to change.
Explain that humans and modern apes share common ancestors rather than humans descending from living monkeys.
Distinguish the scientific meaning of "theory" (well-supported explanation) from the everyday meaning ("mere guess").

beforeReading: Ask learners to notice small inherited differences in the classroom (such as earlobe attachment or thumb bend) to introduce natural variation.

whileReading: Pause after page 5 to reinforce why an individual pale beetle cannot turn dark brown by trying.
Pause after page 10 to draw a simple family tree showing grandparents → two parents (siblings) → two cousins.
afterReading: Classroom simulation: scatter 20 green paper dots and 20 yellow paper dots on a green cloth; give a "bird" 10 seconds to pick dots, then double the survivors to model natural selection over 3 generations.
discussion: Why is inherited variation necessary before natural selection can happen?
How does the cousin analogy help explain what "common ancestor" means?
Why do doctors warn against stopping antibiotic medicine halfway through a course?
reflection: What is one misconception you used to have that became clearer when you looked at the evidence?

mathsExtension.task: In Generation 1, a beetle population has 50 dark beetles and 50 pale beetles (100 total). What percentage is dark?
By Generation 10, 85 out of 100 beetles are dark. By how many percentage points did the dark beetles increase?

support: Use the 4-step sequencing cards to trace Variation → Survival → Reproduction → Generation Shift.
stretch: Research one fossil discovery in Africa and explain what it reveals about ancient environments.

culturalNotes: Yaa (girl born on Thursday), Abena (girl born on Tuesday), and Kwame (boy born on Saturday) are Akan day names.
Set in Accra’s Museum of Science and Technology context.

factCheck.claim: Natural selection acts on heritable variation across generations; individual organisms do not evolve in their own lifetimes out of need or desire.
factCheck.explanation: Mutations and genetic recombination occur prior to selection; differential reproductive success changes allele frequencies in a population over generations.
factCheck.reference: UC Museum of Paleontology — Understanding Evolution (evolution.berkeley.edu); National Academy of Sciences (1998), Teaching About Evolution and the Nature of Science.

factCheck.claim: Humans did not evolve from living monkeys or modern apes; humans and modern apes share distant common ancestors.
factCheck.explanation: Extant primates occupy contemporary tips of the phylogenetic tree; hominins diverged from the common ancestor shared with Pan (chimpanzees/bonobos) in Africa ~6–8 million years ago.
factCheck.reference: Smithsonian Institution National Museum of Natural History — What Does It Mean to Be Human? (humanorigins.si.edu).
factCheck.analogyNote: The cousin/grandparent analogy accurately illustrates branching descent (cladogenesis) vs linear ladder misconceptions.

factCheck.claim: In science, a theory is a comprehensive, well-substantiated explanation of nature supported by independent lines of evidence, not a mere guess.
factCheck.explanation: Scientific theories integrate laws, facts, and tested hypotheses across paleontology, comparative anatomy, biogeography, and molecular genetics.
factCheck.reference: American Association for the Advancement of Science (AAAS) & National Academy of Sciences — Science, Evolution, and Creationism.

characters: Adwoa: an eight-year-old Ghanaian girl with neat braided puffs and red hair beads, wearing a bright coral-orange dress and brown sandals, carrying a woven market basket.
Mama: Adwoa’s warm mother wearing a blue-and-yellow wax-print wrapper and headscarf.
Auntie Dede: a busy, friendly market vegetable seller wearing a red-and-gold head-tie and cloth apron.

pages.brief: Sunny Ghanaian home courtyard: Mama (blue-and-yellow wax-print dress) handing a twenty-cedi note and woven basket to eight-year-old Adwoa (braided puffs with red beads, coral-orange dress).
pages.narration: Warm and encouraging. Emphasise "twenty-cedi note" and "Count the prices and your change carefully".

pages.brief: At Auntie Dede’s colourful vegetable stall, Adwoa holds three fresh green bunches of kontomire leaves and counts on her fingers while Auntie Dede smiles.
pages.narration: Clear, rhythmic counting: "Two, four, six. Three bunches cost six cedis."

pages.brief: Auntie Dede pouring shiny red tomatoes from a small measure bowl into Adwoa’s woven basket; Adwoa thinking carefully.
pages.narration: Slow and clear on the addition: "Six cedis... plus five cedis... makes eleven cedis."

pages.brief: Close view of Adwoa placing a neat white packet of salt (no text) into her woven basket beside the green kontomire leaves and red tomatoes.
pages.narration: Count up clearly: "Twelve, thirteen, fourteen!"

pages.brief: Adwoa holding out her twenty-cedi note at the busy stall while two other market shoppers wait beside Auntie Dede.
pages.narration: Quiet and confident as Adwoa works out the subtraction.

pages.brief: Busy market scene: Auntie Dede turning toward waiting shoppers while pressing two banknotes into Adwoa’s hand.
pages.narration: Brisk, busy market pace.

pages.brief: Under the dappled shade of a neem tree at the market edge, Adwoa stops with her basket and looks closely at the two banknotes in her open palm.
pages.narration: Surprised discovery, then slow, clear arithmetic: "Five cedis plus five cedis was ten cedis... Ten minus six is four."

pages.brief: Adwoa walking past a mango stall with a determined, honest expression, heading straight back toward Auntie Dede’s vegetable stall.
pages.narration: Brief pause on the temptation of the mangoes, then warm resolve.

teacherGuide.overview: A Primary 2–3 mathematics and character story set in a Ghanaian market. Learners practise multiplication by 2, multi-step addition within 20, subtraction to find change from 20 cedis, and the value of honesty when an error occurs.
learningGoals: Calculate the total cost of multiple items using skip-counting and addition within 20 cedis.
Find the correct change from a 20-cedi note by subtracting or counting up.
Identify a calculation discrepancy (10 − 6 = 4 cedis) and explain why returning extra change is honest.

beforeReading: Show learners paper play-money (1, 2, 5, 10 and 20 cedi notes/coins) and practise making 6 cedis and 14 cedis.
whileReading: Pause after page 4 and let every child check Adwoa’s total: 6 + 5 + 3 = 14 cedis.
Pause after page 7 and ask how Adwoa knew she had 4 cedis too much.
afterReading: Set up a classroom market corner where pairs take turns being the buyer (with 20 cedis) and the shopkeeper checking the change together.
discussion: How did doing the maths in her head before paying help Adwoa notice the mistake?
Why was it tempting to keep the four cedis, and what helped Adwoa choose honesty?
reflection: Have you ever found something or received extra change that was not yours? What did you do?

6 cedis + 5 cedis + 3 cedis = ?
Change from 20 cedis when spending 14 cedis = ?

culturalNotes: Adwoa is an Akan day name for a girl born on Monday.

Confirm language of origin and meaning before it appears in teacher notes.

pages.brief: Kwaku smiling as he drops three coins into the slot of his wooden susu box, with one coin beside a small envelope and one coin in his hand.

pages.brief: Sunny afternoon near school: two boys watch a bright plastic spinning top on the ground while Kwaku smiles calmly and steps back without buying.
pages.narration: Lively for the friends, then calm and steady for Kwaku’s choice.

pages.brief: Cosy evening at home with rain outside the window: Maame and Papa sitting together calmly over their household notebook under a warm lamp while Kwaku watches.
pages.narration: Gentle, respectful tone.

pages.brief: Medium close shot: Papa placing a warm, reassuring hand on Kwaku’s shoulder, looking him in the eye with dignity and kindness while Maame smiles supportively.

pages.brief: Sunny Saturday morning: Kwaku sitting at the table with his wooden susu box and six neat groups of तीन tally marks in his notebook.

pages.brief: Kwaku arranging eighteen coins in six neat stacks of three on the wooden table while six-year-old Ama (yellow hair ribbons) claps with delight.

teacherGuide.overview: A Primary 4–5 financial literacy and character story set in Kumasi. Teaches needs vs wants, a simple Save-Spend-Share budget, multiplication/subtraction with Ghana cedis, and explicitly affirms the dignity of hard-working families facing external economic challenges.
learningGoals: Distinguish between essential needs and optional wants.
Create a simple Save-Spend-Share budget and calculate savings over multiple weeks.
Explain why financial hardship is caused by real-world circumstances (such as weather, transport or prices) and never measures a person’s worth or character.

beforeReading: Ask: "What is a susu box, and why does having a slot on top help someone save?"
Discuss the difference between something we need for school and something we want for fun.
whileReading: After page 4, verify that Kwaku’s budget adds up to 5 cedis (3 + 1 + 1 = 5).
After page 7, discuss Papa’s words about dignity, hard work, and why we never judge people by their money.

discussion: What helped Kwaku say no to the four-cedi spinning top on Tuesday?
Why was Papa’s message on page 7 so important for Kwaku to hear?
How did keeping 3 cedis in the box after buying the geometry set help Kwaku’s next goal?
reflection: What is one non-money way you can support your family or a friend when times are busy or difficult?

mathsExtension.task: Kwaku saves 3 cedis a week for 6 weeks. How much does he save?
He also puts 1 cedi a week into his sharing envelope for 6 weeks. How much is in the envelope?
Total earned over 6 weeks at 5 cedis per week = ?

support: Count in threes on a number line up to 18 (3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18).
stretch: If Kwaku wants to save 27 cedis for a dictionary at 3 cedis per week, how many weeks will it take? (9 weeks, or 8 weeks if he starts with his 3 leftover cedis!)

Susu boxes (wooden or metal boxes) are a well-known household savings tradition across Ghana.

characters: Kwame: a cheerful six-year-old Ghanaian boy with short cropped hair and a bright yellow-and-green traditional tunic shirt and brown sandals.
Nana Yaw: Kwame’s kind grandfather with a short white beard, wearing a rich blue-and-gold cloth wrapped over his shoulder.

pages.narration: Warm and rhythmic. Gentle wonder on "Can a drum really talk, Nana?"

pages.brief: Close view of Nana Yaw’s hands holding two L-shaped curved wooden drumsticks over the two leather drumheads of the atumpan pair, while Kwame watches closely.
pages.narration: Perform "kon-kon" in a slightly lower tone and "ka-la" in a slightly higher tone.

pages.brief: Kwame eagerly tapping the drums too fast while seven-year-old Cousin Esi (red patterned dress) covers her ears and giggles playfully.
pages.narration: Playful and fast on "Bam-bam-bam!", then light laughter.

pages.brief: Tender close two-shot: Nana Yaw resting his hands gently over Kwame’s small hands holding the curved drumsticks, both smiling calmly.
pages.narration: Slow, calm, and rhythmic on "Listen with your ears. Listen with your heart."

pages.brief: On the courtyard veranda, Nana Yaw points to a smaller hourglass-shaped lunna drum with leather tension cords and a tall painted cylindrical drum while Kwame and Esi admire them.
pages.narration: Warm and appreciative of Ghana’s diverse cultures.

pages.brief: Nana Yaw playing the two atumpan drums with the curved sticks while Kwame stands still with his eyes closed, listening carefully to the beat.
pages.narration: Clear, steady drum rhythm: "Kon-kon, ka-la! Kon-kon, ka-la!"

pages.brief: Kwame holding the two curved L-shaped sticks with focus and joy, tapping the atumpan drums cleanly while Nana Yaw and Esi clap in rhythm.
pages.narration: Confident, steady beat matching Nana Yaw’s rhythm.

pages.brief: Joyful courtyard gathering in golden afternoon sunlight: neighbours smiling and clapping as Kwame and Nana Yaw stand together by the atumpan drums.
pages.narration: Warm, celebratory, and gentle at the close. Pause before "The end".

teacherGuide.overview: An early-years and lower-primary story introducing the Akan atumpan talking drums while highlighting Ghana’s broader musical diversity (including the Dagomba lunna and Ewe atsimevu) and the social-emotional skill of attentive listening.
learningGoals: Listen to and echo a simple low-high rhythmic pattern (kon-kon, ka-la).
Explain that the Akan atumpan uses two drums (low and high tones) played with curved sticks.
Recognise that Ghana has many distinct cultural and drumming traditions across different regions.

beforeReading: Play a quick "Listen and Echo" clapping game: clap a 4-beat pattern and ask learners to wait until you finish before echoing.
whileReading: Invite learners to tap their knees gently for the low "kon-kon" and clap their hands for the high "ka-la" on pages 2, 6 and 7.
afterReading: Ask learners to share the name of a drum, song or dance from their own family or community.
discussion: Why did Kwame’s first try sound messy?
How can a drum "talk" without using a mouth? (By matching the high and low tones of a tonal language.)
What three drums from different parts of Ghana did Nana Yaw mention?
reflection: What does "Listen with your ears, listen with your heart" mean in our classroom?

mathsExtension.task: The rhythm "Kon-kon, ka-la" has 2 low beats and 2 high beats. How many beats is that in one call?
If Kwame plays the 4-beat call 2 times, how many beats does he play in all?

support: Clap the rhythm slowly together as a whole class before answering the comprehension questions.
stretch: Create your own 4-beat greeting pattern using low knee-taps and high hand-claps and teach it to a partner.

culturalNotes: Kwame (Saturday) and Yaw (Thursday) are Akan day names; Esi is a Fante/Akan day name for a girl born on Sunday; Akwaaba is the Akan word for welcome.

The atumpan is played in pairs (male low-toned drum and female high-toned drum) with two L-shaped sticks; the lunna (dondo) is an hourglass tension drum famous in Dagbon/northern Ghana; the atsimevu is the master drum in Ewe ensembles.
localiseThis: Invite a local musician or cultural teacher to demonstrate an instrument from your school’s community.

characters: Kwabena: an eleven-year-old Ghanaian boy in Primary 6, wearing a bright mustard-yellow polo shirt, khaki shorts and sandals, carrying a small magnifying glass and green field notebook.
Afia: his ten-year-old cousin in Primary 5, wearing a coral-pink patterned top and denim skirt, braided hair with white beads, observant and curious.
Nana Osei: Afia’s grandfather in Abono village, a respected elder wearing a blue-and-brown traditional cloth over his shoulder.
Dr Boateng: a male Ghanaian geologist from Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology (KNUST), wearing a light khaki field vest, glasses and sun hat.

narrationPlan.voice: Warm, clear Ghanaian English storyteller (`Kore`). Respectful elder cadence for Nana Osei, enthusiastic scientific tone for Dr Boateng.
narrationPlan.pace: Medium (about 125 words per minute).
notes: Use phonetic hints for Bosomtwe, Kwabena, Afia, Boateng, and padua while keeping written text in standard spelling.

teacherGuide.overview: Set at Lake Bosomtwe in the Ashanti Region, this story helps Upper Primary learners distinguish between respected cultural oral traditions (how communities relate to and conserve a sacred place) and empirical geological evidence (how a Pleistocene meteorite impact carved the crater 1.07 million years ago and preserved a million-year West African climate archive).
learningGoals: Explain how a meteorite impact formed the Lake Bosomtwe crater approximately 1.07 million years ago.
Identify real geological evidence for an impact crater: circular rim, shocked quartz in breccia, and Ivory Coast tektites.
Explain how annual sediment layers at the bottom of a closed (endorheic) lake record past climate changes.
Respectfully distinguish traditional cultural stories and conservation practices from testable geological explanations.

subjectLinks.subject: Science (Upper Primary)
subjectLinks.link: Earth science, rocks, landforms, and evidence of past environmental change.

subjectLinks.subject: Our World Our People / Social Studies
subjectLinks.link: Major physical features of Ghana (Lake Bosomtwe) and traditional environmental conservation.

subjectLinks.subject: English Language
subjectLinks.link: Informational and narrative reading comprehension, scientific vocabulary.

beforeReading: Locate the Ashanti Region and Lake Bosomtwe (about 30 km south-east of Kumasi) on a map of Ghana.
Ask learners: "Have you ever seen a photograph of craters on the Moon? Could a rock from space make a crater on Earth too?"
whileReading: Pause after page 3 to discuss how the traditional rule against iron boats and loud motors also helps protect the lake from oil pollution and overfishing.
Pause after page 8 to trace the direction from Lake Bosomtwe westward to Côte d’Ivoire where tektites landed.
afterReading: Compare the two questions: "How did people come to revere and care for Lake Bosomtwe?" (cultural history) and "What physical process carved the 10.5 km rock basin?" (geological science).
discussion: Why did scientists rule out the idea that Lake Bosomtwe is a volcanic crater?
How can tiny crystals inside a rock or glassy pebbles in Côte d’Ivoire act as clues to an event that happened over a million years ago?
Why are the mud layers at the bottom of Lake Bosomtwe compared to pages in a history book?
reflection: How can traditional community rules and modern environmental science work together to protect Ghana’s lakes and forests today?

mathsExtension.task: The outer crater rim around Lake Bosomtwe is about 10.5 km wide, while the water surface today is about 8.5 km wide. What is the difference between the crater rim width and the water width?
The meteorite that formed the crater was about 500 metres wide. How many metres are in 1 kilometre, and what fraction of a kilometre is 500 metres?
mathsExtension.answer: 1,000 metres = 1 kilometre; 500 metres is 1/2 (0.5) of a kilometre.

support: Use a bowl and a cup of water to show what a "closed lake" (endorheic basin) means: water enters as rain and leaves only by evaporation.
stretch: Write a short field report explaining three clues you would look for as a geologist to tell an impact crater apart from a volcano.

culturalNotes: Lake Bosomtwe is sacred in Ashanti tradition. The oral tradition of the hunter Akora Bompe and his dog from Asaman following an antelope (twe) is presented respectfully as cultural heritage, never confused with geological age.
The traditional wooden plank craft is called a padua, propelled with flat wooden hand pads.
localiseThis: Connect to any notable rock formations, hills, rivers, or sacred groves in your own district and discuss both their cultural story and geological origin.

whatWeKnow: Lake Bosomtwe occupies a 10.5 km wide meteorite impact crater formed approximately 1.07 million years ago in crystalline Birimian rocks.
Shocked quartz in suevite breccia and radiometrically matched Ivory Coast tektites confirm an extraterrestrial hypervelocity impact.
Deep sediment cores drilled in 2004 (ICDP) preserve over 1 million years of West African monsoon and Sahara dust history.
whatWeAreStillDiscovering: Scientists continue analysing microscopic pollen, charcoal, and chemical isotopes in the deep lake cores to understand how rapid climate shifts affected early human habitats in West Africa.
Hydrologists are actively studying how modern warming and land-use changes around the rim affect the lake’s water balance and native cichlid fish species.

investigation.title: Model an Impact Crater in a Tray
materials: A wide shallow basin or cardboard tray
Dry gari, cornflour, or clean fine sand (about 4 cm deep)
A thin dusting of cocoa powder or dark soil on top
Two or three smooth pebbles or marbles of different sizes
A ruler
steps: Spread a 4 cm layer of gari or fine sand smoothly in the tray and sprinkle a very thin dark layer of cocoa powder or dark soil on top.
Drop a small pebble from shoulder height straight down into the tray and measure the width of the circular crater rim.
Observe where the lighter lower layer was thrown outward (like tektites and ejecta rays).
Gently toss a pebble at a slight angle and notice that the crater still forms a nearly round bowl!
investigation.whatToNotice: Even when a pebble hits at a moderate angle, the shock wave pushes material outward in all directions to make a circular rim with a raised edge.
investigation.safetyNote: Drop pebbles gently downward into the tray placed on the ground; stand back slightly so sand or powder does not splash near eyes, and wash hands afterwards.

factCheck.claim: Lake Bosomtwe was formed approximately 1.07 million years ago by a meteorite impact producing a ~10.5 km crater.
factCheck.explanation: Argon-argon dating of Ivory Coast tektites and impact glasses, combined with geophysical and drilling studies of the Bosomtwe structure, establish an impact age of 1.07 Myr.
factCheck.reference: Koeberl, C., Milkereit, B., Overpeck, J. T., Scholz, C. A., Amoako, P. Y. O., Boamah, D., Danuor, S. et al. (2007). An international and multidisciplinary drilling project into a young complex impact structure: The 2004 Bosomtwe crater drilling project. Meteoritics & Planetary Science, 42(4–5), 483–511.

factCheck.claim: Shocked quartz in impact breccia and Ivory Coast tektites provide conclusive geological evidence of hypervelocity impact.
factCheck.explanation: Planar deformation features in quartz require shock pressures >5–10 GPa that volcanic processes on Earth cannot generate; Ivory Coast tektites have identical chemical and isotopic signatures to the Birimian target rocks at Bosomtwe.
factCheck.reference: Boamah, D., & Koeberl, C. (2003). Geology and geochemistry of shallow drill cores from the Bosomtwe impact crater, Ghana. Meteoritics & Planetary Science, 38(8), 1137–1159; UNESCO Biosphere Reserve Nomination Dossier for Lake Bosomtwe.

reviewerNotes: Confirm Akan tone and final vowel quality.
Confirm local Ashanti Twi pronunciation around Abono/Lake Bosomtwe.

teacherGuide.overview: Set at a marine research laboratory in Tema on the Gulf of Guinea coast, this JHS story takes learners on a remotely operated vehicle (ROV) dive through the ocean’s pelagic zones, explaining hydrostatic pressure, the biochemistry and ecological roles of bioluminescence, and chemosynthetic ecosystems at deep-sea hydrothermal vents.
learningGoals: Compare the sunlit (epipelagic), twilight (mesopelagic), and midnight (bathypelagic) ocean zones in terms of light, temperature, and hydrostatic pressure.
Explain how bioluminescence works chemically (luciferin + luciferase + oxygen) and describe three survival functions (luring prey, startling predators, counter-illumination camouflage).
Contrast photosynthesis at the ocean surface with chemosynthesis at deep-sea hydrothermal vents.
Distinguish established marine biology facts from open questions about unmapped deep-sea ecosystems.

afterReading: Have learners sketch a vertical chart of the ocean zones showing where sunlight ends and how organisms adapt in each layer.
discussion: Why is bioluminescence called "cold light", and how is it different from a glowing hot metal wire?
Why did scientists before 1977 assume that almost no complex life could thrive on the deep ocean floor without food falling from the sunlit surface?
Why should humanity be careful about disturbing or mining deep-sea hydrothermal vents before scientists finish studying the species that live there?

mathsExtension.task: Water pressure increases by about 1 atmosphere for every 10 metres of depth, plus 1 atmosphere of air pressure at the surface. What is the total pressure in atmospheres at 200 metres depth?
If a deep-sea ROV dives at a steady speed of 30 metres per minute, how many minutes will it take to reach 3,000 metres?

support: Use a clear bottle of water and a torch covered with blue cloth layers to model how light dims as depth increases.

whatWeKnow: Sunlight sufficient for photosynthesis penetrates only the upper ~200 metres (the photic/epipelagic zone) of the ocean.
Roughly 75% of pelagic animals between 200 m and 4,000 m produce bioluminescence via luciferin-luciferase chemical reactions or symbiotic bacteria.
Hydrothermal vents (discovered in 1977) support thriving ecosystems powered by chemosynthetic microbes oxidizing hydrogen sulfide rather than using sunlight.
whatWeAreStillDiscovering: Over 80% of the global ocean floor remains unmapped at high acoustic resolution, and marine biologists discover hundreds of new deep-sea species every year.
Biochemists are still investigating unique enzymes and compounds in deep-sea sponges, microbes, and vent organisms that may lead to new medicines.
Ecologists are still studying how deep-sea currents, carbon storage, and potential seabed mining affect fragile abyssal habitats.

investigation.title: See How Water Depth Increases Pressure
materials: An empty 1.5-litre clear plastic water bottle
A ruler and marker
A compass point or nail (handled by the teacher)
Waterproof tape
A bucket or outdoor sink and water
steps: Have the teacher carefully poke three small, equal-sized pinholes in a vertical line down the side of the plastic bottle: one near the top (5 cm down), one in the middle (12 cm down), and one near the bottom (20 cm down).
Cover all three holes with a strip of tape and fill the bottle completely with water (leave the cap off).
Place the bottle at the edge of a table over a bucket or outdoors, peel off the tape all at once, and observe how far each stream of water shoots out horizontally.
investigation.whatToNotice: The stream from the bottom hole shoots out the farthest and fastest because there is a taller column of water pressing down above it—demonstrating how hydrostatic pressure increases with depth!
investigation.safetyNote: Only the teacher should use a sharp point to make the pinholes in the plastic bottle; perform the water test outdoors or over a bucket so floors do not become slippery.

factCheck.claim: About three-quarters of deep pelagic marine organisms produce bioluminescence using luciferin and luciferase.
factCheck.explanation: QuantitativeROV surveys from the surface to 4,000 m show ~76% of macroscopic water-column individuals have bioluminescent capability.
factCheck.reference: Martini, S., & Haddock, S. H. D. (2017). Quantification of bioluminescence from the surface to the deep sea demonstrates its predominance as an ecological trait. Scientific Reports, 7, 45750; NOAA Ocean Exploration — Bioluminescence and Deep-Sea Vents.

factCheck.claim: Hydrothermal vents host ecosystems powered by chemosynthesis rather than photosynthesis, first discovered in 1977.
factCheck.explanation: Discovered along the Galápagos Rift in 1977 and subsequently along the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, vent ecosystems rely on chemoautotrophic bacteria and archaea oxidizing reduced sulfur compounds (H2S).
factCheck.reference: Corliss, J. B. et al. (1979). Submarine thermal springs on the Galápagos Rift. Science, 203(4385), 1073–1083; Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution (WHOI) Hydrothermal Vents Fact Sheet.

teacherGuide.overview: Set near Mole National Park in northern Ghana’s Savannah Region, this Lower Primary story introduces elephant social structure (matriarchal herds), physical adaptations (ears and mud for thermoregulation), infrasound seismic communication, wildlife safety rules, and peaceful human-elephant coexistence using beehive fences.
learningGoals: Describe how African elephant families are led by a matriarch who remembers water and food routes.
Explain how elephants cool themselves using their ears and mud, and how they communicate over long distances using low rumbles (infrasound) and ground vibrations.
State clear wildlife safety rules (never approach wild elephants alone; stay quiet, downwind, and at a safe distance with a ranger).
Explain how beehive fences protect farm crops peacefully while supporting biodiversity.

Why do elephants avoid buzzing honeybees even though an elephant is huge and a bee is tiny?

culturalNotes: Mole National Park is Ghana’s largest wildlife refuge, located in the Savannah Region near Larabanga and Damongo.

localiseThis: Discuss any wildlife reserves, sanctuaries (such as Kakum, Mole, Boabeng-Fiema, or Wechiau), or farm protection methods known in your area.

whatWeKnow: African elephants live in matriarchal family units where the oldest female retains decades of spatial memory for water and food routes.
Elephants produce low-frequency infrasound (<20 Hz) that travels several kilometres through the air and couples into the ground as seismic waves detected via mechanoreceptors in their feet.
Beehive fences and chilli-pepper deterrents significantly reduce crop raiding without harming elephants.
whatWeAreStillDiscovering: Bioacousticians are still decoding the specific meanings of hundreds of different elephant rumbles, postures, and gestures across African populations.
Conservation scientists in West Africa are using satellite collars and genetic studies to map how fragmented forest and savannah elephant corridors can best be reconnected.

investigation.title: Listen to Vibrations Through Solid Wood vs Air
materials: A long wooden classroom desk or table
Your fingertips or a wooden pencil with an eraser end
steps: Have one learner sit at one end of a long wooden desk and tap the wood very softly with a fingertip so their partner standing at the other end can barely hear it through the air.
Now have the partner rest one ear gently flat against the wooden desktop (or press their palm flat on the wood) while the first learner taps with the exact same gentle force.
Compare how clear the tap sounds and feels through the solid wood compared to through the air.
investigation.whatToNotice: Vibrations travel strongly through solid materials like wood and soil—similar to how elephants sense low seismic rumbles through the ground with their feet!
investigation.safetyNote: Tap only very gently with a fingertip or eraser—never bang hard while a classmate’s ear is resting on the desk.

factCheck.claim: Elephants communicate using low-frequency infrasound rumbles and detect seismic ground vibrations through their feet.
factCheck.explanation: Elephant vocalizations include fundamental frequencies of 14–35 Hz that propagate through air and ground; elephant foot pads contain Pacinian corpuscles and acoustic fat pads sensitive to seismic vibrations.
factCheck.reference: O’Connell-Rodwell, C. E. (2007). Keeping an "Ear" to the Ground: Seismic Communication in Elephants. Physiology, 22(4), 287–294; Cornell Lab of Ornithology — Elephant Listening Project.

factCheck.claim: Beehive fences deter elephants from crop fields because elephants fear honeybee stings around their eyes and inside their trunks.
factCheck.explanation: Field trials across Africa demonstrate that elephants actively avoid African honeybees (Apis mellifera scutellata) and emit specific alarm rumbles when hearing bee buzzes.
factCheck.reference: King, L. E., Douglas-Hamilton, I., & Vollrath, F. (2007). African elephants run from the sound of disturbed bees. Current Biology, 17(19), R832–R833; Save the Elephants — Elephants and Bees Project.

teacherGuide.overview: Set at the Ghana Planetarium in Accra, this JHS 2–3 story demystifies black holes using clear physics: debunking the "cosmic vacuum cleaner" myth, explaining escape velocity and the event horizon, presenting four independent lines of observational evidence (stellar orbits around Sagittarius A*, X-ray accretion disks, gravitational waves, and Event Horizon Telescope radio imaging), and highlighting open questions in quantum gravity.
learningGoals: Explain why a black hole is not a cosmic vacuum cleaner and how its gravity at a large distance matches any star of equal mass.
Define escape velocity and explain why light cannot escape from inside the event horizon.
Describe four real astronomical methods used to detect black holes (stellar orbits, accretion-disk X-rays, gravitational waves, and EHT shadow imaging).
Distinguish established relativistic physics from unresolved questions about quantum gravity and the interior of black holes.

subjectLinks.link: Speed, distance, time, large numbers, and inverse-square relationships.

beforeReading: Ask learners: "If you throw a stone straight up, why does it come back down? How fast would you have to launch a rocket so it never falls back to Earth?"
Ask what learners have seen about black holes in movies or cartoons, and list their ideas on the board to test against evidence in the story.
whileReading: Pause after page 3 to check understanding of the Sun-replacement thought experiment.
Pause after page 11 to review the four independent lines of evidence that prove black holes exist even though the interior is dark.
afterReading: Revisit the movie myths on the board and have learners correct each one using scientific evidence from the story.
discussion: Why does Earth not get pulled into the Sun right now, and how does that same principle apply to stars orbiting a black hole at a safe distance?
Where does the stretched-cloth model of spacetime work well, and what are its limitations? (See Analogy Note in the Fact-Check Sheet.)
Why did the Event Horizon Telescope need radio dishes spread across multiple continents to photograph M87* and Sagittarius A*?
reflection: How does learning how scientists detect invisible objects in space change the way you think about solving hard problems using indirect clues?

mathsExtension.task: Earth’s escape velocity is about 11 km/s, while the speed of light is about 300,000 km/s. Approximately how many times faster than Earth’s escape velocity is the speed of light? (Round to the nearest thousand.)
Sagittarius A* is about 26,000 light-years away from Earth. How many years does it take for light or radio waves from the centre of the Milky Way to reach our telescopes?
mathsExtension.answer: 26,000 years (because 1 light-year is the distance light travels in 1 year).

support: Use the stretched-cloth and marble demonstration in class so learners can physically see stable orbits far from the central weight versus capture close to the steep centre.
stretch: Research and write a short paragraph on how Ghana’s 32-metre Kuntunse Radio Telescope contributes to Very Long Baseline Interferometry (VLBI) networks in Africa.

culturalNotes: The Ghana Planetarium in Accra has inspired thousands of Ghanaian schoolchildren in astronomy and space science.
Kofi, Adwoa, and Afia Boateng are Akan names.
localiseThis: Connect to the Ghana Planetarium (Accra) and the Ghana Radio Astronomy Observatory (Kuntunse).

whatWeKnow: Stellar-mass black holes form from the gravitational collapse of massive stars, and supermassive black holes (millions to billions of solar masses) reside at the centres of most large galaxies, including Sagittarius A* in the Milky Way.
Outside the event horizon, a black hole’s gravitational field obeys Einstein’s general relativity (and approximates Newton’s law of gravitation at large distances).
Astronomers have verified black holes through stellar orbits (2020 Nobel Prize in Physics), gravitational waves (LIGO/Virgo, 2015), X-ray accretion disks, and EHT horizon-scale images (2019, 2022).
whatWeAreStillDiscovering: Physicists do not yet have a complete, experimentally verified theory of quantum gravity to describe what replaces the classical "singularity" inside a black hole.
The black hole information paradox—how quantum information is preserved when a black hole slowly evaporates via Hawking radiation—remains an active theoretical question.
Astronomers are still investigating using the James Webb Space Telescope how the earliest supermassive black holes grew so rapidly in the young universe.

investigation.title: Model Gravity and Orbits on a Stretched Cloth
materials: A large plastic basin or bucket (or four students holding the corners of a stretchy cloth taut)
A piece of stretchy T-shirt fabric or lycra cloth
A heavy smooth stone or metal ball
Two or three small glass marbles
steps: Stretch the cloth smoothly and tightly across the top of the basin (or have four learners hold the edges tight and level).
Roll a small marble straight across the flat cloth and observe that it travels in a straight line.
Place the heavy stone in the middle so the cloth curves downward into a funnel, then roll the small marble sideways near the outer edge at a moderate speed so it curves in an orbit around the stone.
Now roll the marble very slowly or aim it closely at the steep central dip and observe how it spirals inward.
investigation.whatToNotice: At a safe distance with enough sideways speed, the marble orbits around the heavy mass without getting "sucked in"; only paths that pass too close or too slowly fall into the steep central well.
investigation.safetyNote: Hold the heavy stone carefully so it does not drop onto toes, and keep small marbles off the floor so nobody slips.

factCheck.claim: Replacing the Sun with a black hole of equal mass would not suck in the Earth; Earth would maintain its orbit.
factCheck.explanation: By Birkhoff’s theorem in general relativity (and Newton’s shell theorem), the external gravitational field at distances much greater than the Schwarzschild radius (r_s ≈ 3 km for 1 solar mass) is identical to that of the Sun.
factCheck.reference: NASA Black Hole Safety & Myths FAQ; Thorne, K. S. (1994), Black Holes and Time Warps.
factCheck.analogyNote: The stretched-cloth analogy helps visualise how mass curves spacetime, but teachers should clarify that real spacetime is 4-dimensional (not a 2D sheet) and balls on a cloth slow down due to friction, whereas space is nearly frictionless.

factCheck.claim: Sagittarius A* (~4 million solar masses) and M87* have been confirmed through stellar orbits, gravitational waves, and Event Horizon Telescope radio interferometry.
factCheck.explanation: Ghez et al. and Genzel et al. tracked star S2 orbiting Sgr A* (2020 Nobel Prize); LIGO detected binary black hole mergers in 2015 (GW150914); the EHT Collaboration published direct shadow images of M87* (2019) and Sgr A* (2022).
factCheck.reference: Event Horizon Telescope Collaboration (2019, 2022), Astrophysical Journal Letters; Nobel Prize in Physics 2017 & 2020 Scientific Background.

teacherGuide.overview: Designed for Primary 1–2 learners, this schoolyard story introduces practical observation and measurement (comparing temperatures in sun vs shade), explains in child-friendly terms how trees cool their surroundings through shade and transpiration/evaporation, and models environmental teamwork through tree planting and care.
learningGoals: Observe and compare temperatures in direct sunlight versus under tree shade.
Explain two ways trees help cool a compound: blocking direct solar rays (shade) and releasing moisture from leaves that evaporates (transpiration).
Identify what young saplings need to survive (water, soil, sunlight, mulch to hold moisture, and protection from browsing animals).
Work cooperatively with classmates to care for the school environment.

beforeReading: Look out of the classroom window and count how many trees are in the school compound.
Ask learners: "Where do you like to stand during midday break on a very hot day? Why?"
whileReading: Pause after page 4 and count up together from 30 to 36 on fingers to find the 6-degree difference.
Pause after page 6 and have learners blow gently on a damp hand to feel how evaporating water cools skin.
afterReading: Take a 5-minute walk around the school compound to identify a sunny spot that would benefit from a shade tree.
discussion: What happens to bare soil when the hot sun shines on it all day with no trees or grass?
Why did the children water the saplings early in the morning and put dry leaves (mulch) around the soil?
Why do young trees in Ghana often need a small fence or basket guard around them?
reflection: What is one thing you and your friends can do this week to care for plants or trees at school or at home?

mathsExtension.task: The temperature in the sun was 36 degrees and the temperature in the shade was 30 degrees. How many degrees cooler was the shade?
Team Green planted 4 saplings. If each sapling needs 2 cans of water in the morning, how many cans of water do they carry altogether?

support: Do the damp-hand cooling test in class: wet the back of one hand with a drop of clean water, keep the other hand dry, wave both gently, and feel which hand feels cooler.
stretch: Draw a labelled picture of a tree showing the roots drinking water, the trunk carrying it up, and the leaves making shade and cool air.

culturalNotes: Neem (Azadirachta indica) and mango trees are among the most common schoolyard and compound shade trees across Ghana; ampe is a beloved Ghanaian jumping and clapping game.
Kwame, Abena, and Akua are Akan day names.
localiseThis: Name the specific shade trees growing in your own school compound (such as neem, mango, acacia, rain tree, or almond tree).

whatWeKnow: Tree canopies intercept incoming solar radiation, reducing surface temperatures beneath them by several degrees Celsius compared to bare sunlit ground.
Trees absorb water through their roots and release water vapour through tiny leaf pores (stomata) in a process called transpiration, which absorbs heat energy and cools surrounding air.
Tree roots bind topsoil and reduce rainwater runoff and erosion on school compounds.
whatWeAreStillDiscovering: Urban foresters and climate scientists in West Africa are studying which native Ghanaian tree species cool towns best while surviving longer dry spells.

investigation.title: Compare Sun and Shade with Two Cups of Water
materials: Two identical plastic cups
Clean water from the same bucket or tap
A sunny spot and a shady spot under a tree or veranda
A classroom thermometer (or clean fingers to compare warmth)
steps: Fill both cups halfway with water from the same bucket so they start at the exact same temperature.
Place Cup A out in direct sunlight and Cup B in the shade under a tree for 30 minutes during morning lessons.
After 30 minutes, bring both cups together and measure the water temperature with a thermometer (or touch the outside of each cup to compare).
investigation.whatToNotice: Cup A from the direct sun feels noticeably warmer than Cup B from the shade, showing how shade blocks solar heat energy!
investigation.safetyNote: Use plastic cups (not breakable glass), and stay in the shade as much as possible when setting out and collecting the cups at midday.

factCheck.claim: Trees cool their surroundings both by blocking direct solar radiation (shade) and through evaporative cooling from transpiration.
factCheck.explanation: Canopy shading reduces surface radiant heating, while latent heat of vaporization during leaf transpiration cools ambient air temperature (typically 2–8 °C cooler surface/local feel depending on soil moisture and canopy density).
factCheck.reference: FAO Urban and Peri-Urban Forestry Guidelines; US EPA — Using Trees and Vegetation to Reduce Heat Islands.

pronunciation.guidance: Candidate: "KWAH-meh". English speakers often say "KWAH-mee"; confirm the final vowel.
reviewerNotes: Confirm final vowel (meh vs mee) and the "kw" onset.

teacherGuide.overview: Set in Koforidua in the Eastern Region, this Upper Primary story integrates scientific observation, fair testing, data representation (bar graphs), verified arithmetic (addition, subtraction, and mean of 5-day rainfall data), and the foundational distinction between daily weather and long-term climate across Ghana’s ecological zones.
learningGoals: Explain why a rain gauge must have straight sides and be placed in an open site away from roofs and trees.
Read and interpret a 5-day rainfall dataset in millimetres, calculate the total (50 mm), range (18 mm − 0 mm), and mean (10 mm/day), and represent the data on a bar graph.
Clearly distinguish between daily weather and long-term climate (30+ year averages).
Describe how rainfall records help farmers and water managers in Ghana.

beforeReading: Ask learners: "If a big bucket and a narrow straight jar stand side by side in the open rain, will the water be deeper in the bucket, deeper in the jar, or the same depth?" (Wait to revisit after page 3!)
whileReading: Pause after page 6 to check the subtraction: 18 mm − 12 mm = 6 mm.
Pause after page 8 to verify the addition (12 + 0 + 18 + 6 + 14 = 50 mm) and division (50 ÷ 5 = 10 mm).
afterReading: Have every learner draw the 5-day bar graph in their exercise book with a ruler, labelling the horizontal axis (Monday to Friday) and the vertical axis (Rainfall in mm, counting by 2s from 0 to 20).
discussion: Why did Monday’s storm seem bigger to Kojo at first even though Wednesday brought more millimetres of rain?
Why do meteorologists empty the rain gauge at the exact same time every morning after recording the reading?
What is the difference between saying "It rained 18 mm on Wednesday" (weather) and saying "Southern Ghana has its major rainy season from April to July" (climate)?
reflection: When Have you changed your mind about an idea after checking real measurements or facts, just like Kojo did?

mathsExtension.task: Using Akosua’s 5-day data (Monday 12 mm, Tuesday 0 mm, Wednesday 18 mm, Thursday 6 mm, Friday 14 mm), how much rain fell on the first three days combined?
If Saturday had 10 mm of rain, what would be the new total for all 6 days, and what would the 6-day mean be?

support: Use centimetre/millimetre rulers so learners can see how small 1 mm is (one-tenth of a centimetre) and mark 12 mm and 18 mm on paper strips.
stretch: Compare two weeks of rainfall data using a double bar chart and write three sentences comparing their totals and averages.

culturalNotes: The Ghana Meteorological Agency (GMet) operates synoptic and agro-meteorological weather stations across all regions of Ghana.
Akosua, Kojo, and Boateng are Akan names; Koforidua is the regional capital of the Eastern Region.
localiseThis: Discuss whether your school is in the southern bimodal rainfall zone (two wet seasons) or the northern unimodal rainfall zone (one wet season), and when farmers in your community plant maize, yam, or millet.

whatWeKnow: Rainfall depth is measured in millimetres using a standard funnel-and-cylinder rain gauge sited in an unobstructed open area.
Weather describes short-term atmospheric conditions (hours to days), whereas climate describes statistical weather patterns over at least 30 years (WMO standard).
Ghana’s seasonal rainfall is driven by the north-south movement of the Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ) / West African Monsoon.
whatWeAreStillDiscovering: Climate scientists at GMet and West African universities are studying how warming oceans in the Gulf of Guinea change the onset dates and intensity of extreme rainfalls for local farmers.

investigation.title: Build a Classroom Rain Gauge and Keep a 5-Day Log
materials: A clear, straight-sided 1.5-litre plastic bottle
Scissors (used by the teacher)
A handful of clean small pebbles or marbles
A plastic ruler marked in millimetres (mm) and waterproof tape
Water and a notebook
steps: Have the teacher cut the top curved shoulder off the plastic bottle (about one-third from the top).

Place a 3 cm layer of pebbles in the bottom of the bottle to weight it down so wind cannot tip it over, and pour water in just to the top of the pebbles—mark that flat water line as your "0 mm" starting line.
Tape a ruler vertically on the outside of the straight-sided bottle with the "0" mark aligned exactly with your starting water line, then invert the cut top into the bottle as a funnel.

Place the gauge in an open spot outdoors during a rainy week, read how many millimetres the water rises above the 0 line at 8:00 a.m. each morning, refill/reset to the 0 line, and draw a 5-day bar graph!
investigation.whatToNotice: Adding pebbles and filling water to a marked 0 line above the uneven bottle base gives a flat, straight-sided starting level so every millimetre of rain is measured accurately.
investigation.safetyNote: Only the teacher should cut the plastic bottle and smooth any sharp plastic edges with tape; never go outside into an open field during active lightning or thunder—wait until the storm has passed to read the gauge.

factCheck.claim: A standard rain gauge measures precipitation depth in millimetres in an unobstructed open location, and climate is defined over a 30-year baseline.
factCheck.explanation: The World Meteorological Organization (WMO) defines precipitation depth in mm (1 mm = 1 litre per square metre) and uses 30-year climatological standard normals to distinguish climate from daily weather.
factCheck.reference: World Meteorological Organization (WMO) Guide to Instruments and Methods of Observation (WMO-No. 8); Ghana Meteorological Agency (GMet) Educational Resources.

pronunciation.guidance: Candidate: "ah-KOH-swah"; a three-syllable "ah-KOH-soo-ah" may be more accurate.
reviewerNotes: Two or three syllables at the end? Please decide.

teacherGuide.overview: Set at Kakum National Park in the Central Region, this Primary 3–4 story introduces the Kakum Canopy Walkway, rainforest canopy habitats, watershed protection for Cape Coast, the economics and ethics of responsible ecotourism, and the accurate distinction between inscribed UNESCO World Heritage Sites and Ghana’s UNESCO Tentative List.
learningGoals: Explain what ecotourism is and state at least three responsible visitor rules in a national park.
Describe why the canopy walkway allows visitors to observe upper-canopy wildlife without destroying the forest floor.
Explain how Kakum’s rainforest protects the Kakum River watershed that supplies drinking water to Cape Coast.
Understand how tourism revenue and local jobs support conservation.

subjectLinks.subject: Our World Our People / Social Studies
subjectLinks.link: Tourist sites in Ghana, environmental conservation, and national heritage.

subjectLinks.subject: Science (Lower/Upper Primary)
subjectLinks.link: Rainforest habitats, water cycle / watersheds, and human impact on ecosystems.

subjectLinks.subject: English Language
subjectLinks.link: Reading comprehension, descriptive vocabulary, and oral communication.

beforeReading: Locate the Central Region, Cape Coast, and Kakum National Park on a map of Ghana.
Ask learners: "If a cousin or friend from another country visited Ghana, what natural place would you be proud to show them, and how would you keep it clean?"
whileReading: Pause after page 4 to note the numbers: 7 bridges, 350 metres total length, up to 40 metres above the forest floor.
Pause after page 8 to trace where visitor money goes (park rangers, trail maintenance, local guides, village artisans).
afterReading: Have learners design a "Welcome to Kakum — Leave Only Footprints" poster listing three rules for visitors.
discussion: Why do more birds and monkeys live high in the rainforest canopy than on the dark forest floor?
How does protecting trees in Kakum help someone turning on a water tap in Cape Coast?
What is the difference between tourism that harms nature (littering, disturbing animals) and ecotourism that protects nature?
reflection: What natural place in your own community—a stream, grove, park, or beach—needs people to care for it the way rangers care for Kakum?

mathsExtension.task: The Kakum Canopy Walkway has 7 bridges with a total length of 350 metres. What is the average length of each bridge if they were equal?
If a school group of 10 children visits the walkway and each child’s ticket is 15 cedis, how much does the group pay in total toward park conservation?

support: Act out the four ecotourism rules from page 2 using simple hand gestures.
stretch: Write a postcard from Jayden to his school in London explaining three things he learned about Ghana’s rainforest.

culturalNotes: Kakum National Park was gazetted as a national park in 1992 and its Canopy Walkway opened in 1995 through collaboration between the Wildlife Division (Forestry Commission), the Ghana Heritage Conservation Trust, and Conservation International.

Accurate heritage note: Ghana’s inscribed UNESCO World Heritage Sites are the Forts and Castles (Volta, Greater Accra, Central and Western Regions, 1979) and the Asante Traditional Buildings (1980). Kakum National Park (Assin Attandanso Reserve) was placed on Ghana’s UNESCO World Heritage Tentative List in 2000.
localiseThis: Connect to the nearest protected forest reserve, wildlife sanctuary, waterfall, or river catchment in your region.

whatWeKnow: Tropical rainforest canopies house the majority of forest biodiversity because sunlight drives flowering and fruiting in the upper tree crowns.
Forested watersheds like Kakum regulate stream flow, filter sediment, and sustain municipal water supplies for Cape Coast and surrounding districts.
whatWeAreStillDiscovering: Canopy biologists are still cataloging hundreds of insect, orchid, and epiphyte species that live exclusively in the high crowns of West African upper-Guinean rainforests.

investigation.title: See How Forest Roots and Leaves Keep Water Clean
materials: Two cut plastic bottle funnels (or two small flowerpots with drainage holes)
Two clear cups
Loose bare soil for Funnel A
Soil covered with dead leaves, grass roots, or moss for Funnel B
A cup of water
steps: Place bare loose soil in Funnel A over Cup A, and soil covered with a thick layer of leaves and roots in Funnel B over Cup B.
Pour the same amount of water slowly over both funnels to imitate rain falling on a bare hill versus a forested Kakum hill.
Compare how muddy or clear the water is in Cup A versus Cup B!
investigation.whatToNotice: The water filtering through the leaves and roots (Funnel B) comes out much clearer and flows more steadily, showing how forest cover protects rivers like the Kakum River!
investigation.safetyNote: Wash hands with soap and clean water after handling soil and leaves, and do not drink the test water.

factCheck.claim: The Kakum Canopy Walkway consists of 7 bridges spanning ~350 metres at heights up to 40 metres, and Kakum is on Ghana’s UNESCO Tentative List while protecting the Kakum River watershed.
factCheck.explanation: Kakum National Park (375 km²) protects the headwaters of the Kakum, Nemimi, and Nbuakosua rivers supplying Cape Coast; it is listed on the UNESCO World Heritage Tentative List (Ref. 1393, submitted 2000).
factCheck.reference: UNESCO World Heritage Centre — Kakum National Park (Assin Attandanso Reserve) Tentative List Ref. 1393; Forestry Commission of Ghana (Wildlife Division).

reviewerNotes: Confirm vowel quality and whether the final syllable is stressed.

teacherGuide.overview: Framed through a guided visit to the Manhyia Palace Museum in Kumasi, this Primary 5–JHS 1 story presents the verified historical context of Nana Yaa Asantewaa (Queen Mother of Ejisu), the 1896 exile of Asantehene Nana Prempeh I, the sacred meaning of the Golden Stool (Sika Dwa Kofi), Governor Frederick Hodgson’s demand on 28 March 1900, and the 1900 War of the Golden Stool, while explicitly teaching learners how historians distinguish primary records and oral traditions from invented dialogue.
learningGoals: Explain the constitutional role of the Queen Mother (Ohemmaa) in Asante governance and identify Nana Yaa Asantewaa as Queen Mother of Ejisu.
Explain why the Golden Stool (Sika Dwa Kofi) is sacred to the Asante nation and why Governor Hodgson’s demand on 28 March 1900 provoked resistance.
Distinguish between verified historical facts, oral traditions of speeches, and modern museum framing.
Reflect on how courage, sacrifice, and unity protect national dignity.

discussion: Why was the Golden Stool never sat upon, and why did Governor Hodgson’s demand show a deep misunderstanding of Asante culture and sovereignty?
What role did women play in leadership and governance in traditional Ghanaian societies as shown by Nana Yaa Asantewaa?
Even though Nana Yaa Asantewaa was eventually captured and exiled to the Seychelles, why do historians consider the defence of the Golden Stool a lasting triumph?
reflection: When is a time in school or community life when standing up for what is right requires quiet courage?

mathsExtension.task: Nana Prempeh I was exiled in 1896 and returned to Kumasi in 1924. How many years was he in exile?
The War of the Golden Stool began in March 1900 and Nana Yaa Asantewaa passed away in the Seychelles in 1921. How many years passed between March 1900 and 1921?

support: Use a visual timeline with four dates: 1896 (Exile of Prempeh I), 28 March 1900 (Hodgson’s demand & Yaa Asantewaa’s leadership), 1921 (Yaa Asantewaa’s passing in Seychelles), and 1924 (Return of Prempeh I).
stretch: Write a short historical essay explaining how comparing British colonial records and Asante oral traditions gives a fuller picture of the 1900 war than reading only one side.

culturalNotes: Nana Yaa Asantewaa (c. 1840–1921) was the Edwesohemmaa (Queen Mother of Ejisu/Edweso). Manhyia Palace Museum in Kumasi preserves royal Asante history and artefacts.
