whatWeKnow: In 1896 British authorities exiled Asantehene Nana Prempeh I; on 28 March 1900 Governor Sir Frederick Hodgson demanded the Golden Stool at Kumasi.

Nana Yaa Asantewaa, Queen Mother of Ejisu, led the 1900 resistance (War of the Golden Stool); she was later exiled to the Seychelles where she died in October 1921, while the Golden Stool was never captured.
whatWeAreStillDiscovering: Ghanaian and international historians continue archiving local family oral histories, photographs from the Seychelles exile, and regional accounts of the 1900 stockade defences across Ashanti towns.

investigation.title: Be a Historian: Compare Two Eyewitness Accounts
materials: Exercise books and pencils
A short 1-minute classroom action (for example, the teacher walks to the board, draws a star, puts down the chalk, and opens a window)
steps: Have the teacher perform a short 4-step action in front of the class without announcing it beforehand.
Ask three learners sitting in different parts of the room to write down what they saw, and ask a fourth learner to interview them and combine the evidence.
Compare the accounts: which details did every witness agree on, and which details were only visible from one angle?
investigation.whatToNotice: Different witnesses notice different details, so historians compare multiple independent accounts and physical clues to reconstruct what truly happened!
investigation.safetyNote: Standard classroom activity; treat every classmate’s written observation respectfully.

factCheck.claim: On 28 March 1900, British Governor Sir Frederick Hodgson demanded the Golden Stool in Kumasi, and Nana Yaa Asantewaa (Queen Mother of Ejisu) led the subsequent resistance.
factCheck.explanation: Hodgson’s demand is documented in British Colonial Office dispatches (Gold Coast Confidential, 1900), and Yaa Asantewaa’s leadership of the 1900 uprising and subsequent exile to the Seychelles (d. 17 October 1921) are established in Ghanaian and imperial historiography.
factCheck.reference: Boahen, A. A. (2003). Yaa Asantewaa and the Asante-British War of 1900–1. James Currey / Sub-Saharan Publishers; Arhin, K. (2000). The Role of Yaa Asantewaa in the 1900 Asante War of Resistance; Manhyia Palace Museum Historical Archives.

teacherGuide.overview: Set on a vegetable farm near Dawhenya on the Accra Plains, this Primary 5–6 story teaches the science and economics of tropical greenhouse farming: photosynthesis, rain and pest protection, the critical scientific distinction between a physical greenhouse structure and the planetary atmospheric greenhouse effect, tropical ventilation and humidity management, drip irrigation, integrated pest management, and a verified Ghana cedi farm budget.
learningGoals: Explain how a greenhouse controls growing conditions (sunlight for photosynthesis, shelter from heavy rain, drip irrigation for roots, mesh netting against pests).

Distinguish clearly between how a farm greenhouse traps warm air physically (suppressing convection/wind) and how Earth’s atmospheric greenhouse effect works (gases absorbing and re-emitting infrared radiation).

Explain realistic limitations and trade-offs: poor ventilation causes severe overheating in Ghana’s climate, pests can still enter without strict hygiene, and construction/maintenance costs require careful budgeting.
Calculate total costs (1,000 cedis), revenue (1,600 cedis), and net profit (600 cedis).

Pause after page 12 to write Uncle Ofori’s budget on the board and check every number together.

discussion: Why is a greenhouse designed for cold European winters dangerous for tomato plants in tropical Ghana unless it has high vents and mesh sides?
Why does drip irrigation save water and reduce leaf diseases compared to splashing water over the whole plant?
Why would a farmer fail if they counted the 1,600 cedis of tomato sales as pure profit without setting aside money for seeds, water, labour, and net repairs?
reflection: What crop grown in your community could benefit from better water management or pest protection?

If a storm tore a section of side netting that cost 150 cedis to repair out of the 600-cedi profit, how much profit would remain?

stretch: Design a simple seasonal budget for a school garden bed growing kontomire or okra, listing expected costs and expected sales.

culturalNotes: Greenhouse vegetable production (especially tomatoes, bell peppers, and cucumbers) has expanded around Dawhenya, Dodowa, Kumasi, and Youth in Greenhouse Enterprise initiatives in Ghana.
Kojo, Ama, and Ofori are Akan names.
localiseThis: Connect to local irrigation schemes (such as Dawhenya, Kpong, Tono, or Vea) or school agricultural plots in your district.

whatWeKnow: Physical greenhouses warm primarily by suppressing convective air mixing with the outside atmosphere, whereas the planetary greenhouse effect is driven by radiative absorption and re-emission by greenhouse gases (CO2, H2O, CH4).
In tropical climates, passive roof-and-side ventilation and insect-exclusion netting are essential to keep daytime temperatures below ~32–35 °C where tomato pollen viability drops.
Drip irrigation significantly increases water-use efficiency and reduces foliar fungal pathogens compared to overhead watering.
whatWeAreStillDiscovering: Agronomists in Ghana are breeding heat-tolerant tomato varieties and testing solar-powered cooling fans and locally made cocopeat growing media to lower greenhouse startup costs for young farmers.

investigation.title: Test How Ventilation Controls Heat in a Mini-Greenhouse
materials: Three identical clear plastic bowls or cut clear plastic bottles
Three small strips of cardboard or soil beds
A sunny windowsill or outdoor table
A classroom thermometer
steps: Place Bowl A upside down completely closed over a cardboard base in the sun (no ventilation).
Place Bowl B upside down with two small gaps propped open at the bottom and a vent hole at the top (ventilated greenhouse), and leave Base C uncovered in the open air.
After 15 minutes in the sun, measure the air temperature inside Bowl A, inside Bowl B, and on open Base C.
investigation.whatToNotice: Closed Bowl A becomes dangerously hot very quickly, while ventilated Bowl B stays sheltered from wind while keeping a moderate temperature closer to the healthy range for plants!
investigation.safetyNote: Teacher should pre-cut any vent holes in plastic bottles; do not leave sealed containers in extreme heat for long periods.

factCheck.claim: A physical greenhouse warms primarily by preventing convective heat loss (trapping warm air), whereas the atmospheric greenhouse effect operates via infrared radiative absorption by greenhouse gases.
factCheck.explanation: As demonstrated by R. W. Wood (1909) and standard atmospheric physics, a physical greenhouse suppresses air convection; atmospheric warming is governed by infrared-active gases.
factCheck.reference: IPCC Sixth Assessment Report (AR6) WGI Glossary & FAQ; American Meteorological Society Education Resources.
factCheck.analogyNote: Calling atmospheric warming the "greenhouse effect" is a historical metaphor; teachers should highlight Uncle Ofori’s explanation on pages 5–6 so pupils do not think there is a literal glass roof in the sky.

factCheck.claim: In tropical climates like Ghana, tomato fruit set fails when daytime temperatures exceed ~35–38 °C, making ventilation, drip irrigation, and integrated pest scouting essential.
factCheck.explanation: High heat (>35 °C) impairs pollen germination in Solanum lycopersicum; tropical net-houses require passive ridge ventilation and IPM scouting.
factCheck.reference: FAO (2017). Good Agricultural Practices for Greenhouse Vegetable Production in the Mediterranean and Tropical Regions; CSIR–Crops Research Institute (Ghana) Vegetable Production Guides.

teacherGuide.overview: Set in Sunyani, this Primary 4–6 character and values story portrays a Ghanaian Christian family that reveres God as Supreme while teaching a vital life lesson: genuine faith inspires diligence, honesty, preparation, and service—never replacing study, planning, or medical care. It also models warm interfaith respect between Christian and Muslim classmates and explicitly affirms that poverty or misfortune never results from insufficient faith.
learningGoals: Explain how faith, gratitude, and personal responsibility (studying, planning, asking questions) work together harmoniously.
Demonstrate honesty, humility, and perseverance when correcting a mistake.
Practice mutual respect and teamwork across Ghana’s religious diversity.
Add simple fractions with unlike denominators (1/2 + 1/4 = 2/4 + 1/4 = 3/4).

teacherGuide.overview: Serving as both a standalone JHS entrepreneurship story and a direct sequel to Efua’s Honest Business, this 12-page story teaches essential real-world financial management: why sales growth can trigger a cash-flow crisis, how to separate revenue from variable and fixed costs, how credit sales affect cash flow versus accounting profit, why emergency reserves matter for external shocks (like rainstorms or price rises), and why ethical marketing outperforms deception.
learningGoals: Distinguish clearly between revenue (total sales), expenses (variable + fixed costs), and net profit.
Explain the difference between accounting profit and cash flow, showing how unpaid credit sales can starve a profitable business of working capital.
Calculate unit variable costs, total costs, net profit, and net cash flow from a realistic Ghana cedi scenario.
Evaluate ethical versus deceptive responses to rising business costs.

beforeReading: Ask learners: "If a shopkeeper sells 200 cedis worth of goods in a week, did the shopkeeper make 200 cedis of profit? Why or why not?"

afterReading: Have learners work in pairs to calculate Efua’s new weekly profit after she lowers her ingredient cost from 1.10 cedis to 0.90 cedis per pack (see Maths Extension).
discussion: Why do many promising small businesses get into trouble right when their orders suddenly grow larger?

mathsExtension.task: In the following week, Efua sells 100 packs at 2 cedis each (200 cedis revenue). Her wholesale ingredient cost is now 0.90 cedis per pack (90 cedis), there is no taxi emergency (0 cedis), and fixed costs are 25 cedis. What are her new total expenses and new weekly profit?
mathsExtension.answer: Total expenses = 90 + 25 = 115 cedis; New profit = 200 − 115 = 85 cedis.

mathsExtension.task: Under her new rule, the school canteen orders 30 packs (60 cedis total) and pays a 50% deposit upfront. How much cash does Efua receive immediately when the order is placed?

teacherGuide.overview: Set at Cape Coast Castle in the Central Region, this JHS 1–3 history and citizenship story models a respectful, evidence-based educational visit led by the Ghana Museums and Monuments Board (GMMB). It establishes West Africa’s pre-colonial achievements, traces the 1653 Swedish and 1664 British history of the fortress, confronts the injustice of the transatlantic slave trade without graphic sensationalism or invented survivor quotes, explains the symbolic "Door of No Return" / "Door of Return", and connects historical memory to universal human rights.
learningGoals: Explain the historical significance of Cape Coast Castle as an inscribed UNESCO World Heritage Site managed by the Ghana Museums and Monuments Board.
Trace how coastal trade shifted from gold and timber to the transatlantic slave trade linking West Africa, the Americas/Caribbean, and Europe.
Explain why visitors from Ghana, the African diaspora, and around the world visit Cape Coast Castle to remember and reconnect.
Articulate why preserving painful historical evidence protects human rights and dignity today.

Pause after page 10 to discuss the meaning of both sides of the portal: "Door of No Return" (historical reality of forced departure) and "Door of Return" (1998 Emancipation Day welcome to the diaspora).
afterReading: Discuss Esi’s closing sentence on page 12: how does remembering past injustice help us protect freedom and human rights today?
discussion: Why did Mr Mensah point out the architectural contrast between the dark lower chambers and the airy governor’s rooms and chapel directly above?
Why do descendants of enslaved Africans in the Americas and the Caribbean travel thousands of kilometres to stand inside Cape Coast and Elmina Castles?
How can young Ghanaians welcome diaspora visitors while also protecting and maintaining Ghana’s historical monuments?
reflection: What does the word "dignity" mean to you in how we treat classmates, strangers, and people from every background?

support: Use a world map to trace the three sides of the Atlantic trade triangle and review the five glossary terms before reading.

culturalNotes: Cape Coast Castle (along with Elmina Castle and other coastal fortifications) was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1979 under "Forts and Castles, Volta, Greater Accra, Central and Western Regions" and is conserved by the Ghana Museums and Monuments Board (GMMB).
Avoid role-playing or dramatising the suffering of enslaved captives in class; keep all activities analytical, empathetic, and respectful.
localiseThis: Connect to any historical monuments, museums, or heritage sites preserved by the Ghana Museums and Monuments Board in your region.

whatWeKnow: Inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1979, Cape Coast Castle grew from a 1555 Portuguese lodge and 1653 Swedish fort (Carolusborg) into the British headquarters on the Gold Coast (1664–1877) and a major holding fortress of the transatlantic slave trade.
Historians estimate that over 12.5 million African men, women, and children were forced onto transatlantic slave ships between the 16th and 19th centuries.
whatWeAreStillDiscovering: Archaeologists, historians, and geneticists in Ghana and the diaspora continue researching archival shipping manifests, oral histories along inland slave routes (such as Assin Manso and Salaga), and conservation methods to protect coastal stone monuments from sea-level rise and salt erosion.

investigation.title: Heritage Conservation Observation: How Salt Air Affects Stone and Metal
materials: Two small pieces of chalk or porous limestone/brick
Two small iron nails (clean, handled carefully)
Two shallow dishes: Dish A with plain tap water, Dish B with salty water (1 spoon of salt stirred in)
Observation notebook
steps: Place one piece of chalk/stone and one nail in Dish A (fresh water) and the second pair in Dish B (salt water), then lift them onto paper towels to dry in the air each day for 3 days.
Observe how salt crystals form inside the pores of the chalk/stone as water evaporates and how salt speeds up rust on iron.
investigation.whatToNotice: Salt water and sea spray speed up rusting and leave salt crystals that weather porous stone and lime mortar—showing why GMMB conservators must work continually to preserve coastal monuments like Cape Coast Castle!
investigation.safetyNote: Wash hands after handling rusty nails or salt solutions, and dispose of rusted nails safely with the teacher.

factCheck.claim: Cape Coast Castle was expanded as Carolusborg by the Swedes in 1653, taken by the British in 1664, and inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1979 under the stewardship of the Ghana Museums and Monuments Board.
factCheck.explanation: Historical and architectural documentation by GMMB and UNESCO World Heritage Convention (Ref. 34) confirm the 1653 Swedish construction under Heinrich Caarlof, 1664 British capture, and 1979 UNESCO inscription.
factCheck.reference: UNESCO World Heritage Centre — Forts and Castles, Volta, Greater Accra, Central and Western Regions (Ref. 34); Anquandah, J. (1999). Castles & Forts of Ghana. Ghana Museums and Monuments Board; Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade Database (SlaveVoyages.org).

Practise fair teamwork and honest record-keeping.

investigation.title: One Basket vs Three Baskets Simulation
materials: Ten counters (representing 100 cedis each = 1,000 cedis), three cups labelled Stock A, Stock B, and Bond, and a coin to flip.
steps: Scenario 1 (Undiversified): Put all 10 counters (1,000 cedis) into Stock B alone. When Stock B drops by 10%, calculate your ending total (900 cedis, a 100-cedi loss).
Scenario 2 (Diversified): Place 4 counters in Stock A (+12.5% → 450 cedis), 2 counters in Stock B (-10% → 180 cedis), and 4 counters in Bond (+15% → 460 cedis).
Add the three cups in Scenario 2 (450 + 180 + 460 = 1,090 cedis) and compare with Scenario 1.

investigation.title: Risk-Pooling Dice Simulation
materials: Six groups of pupils, one 6-sided die, and 60 counters (10 counters per group).
steps: Round 1 (No Insurance Pool): Each group keeps its 10 counters. Roll the die—whichever group number is rolled suffers a "storm loss" of 12 counters (more than they have!).
Round 2 (Risk Pool): Each of the 6 groups contributes 3 counters (premium) into a central Umbrella Pool (6 × 3 = 18 counters in the pool, leaving 7 counters per group).
Roll the die for the storm loss of 12 counters: the Umbrella Pool pays 11 counters and the affected group pays a 1-counter deductible—every group stays afloat!

investigation.title: Year-by-Year Compounding Seed Lab
materials: 100 dried beans or maize kernels and 3 small bowls labelled "Start (Year 0)", "End of Year 1", and "End of Year 2".
steps: Count 100 beans into the Year 0 bowl (representing 1,000 cedis, where 1 bean = 10 cedis).
For Year 1 at 10% growth, add 10% of 100 beans (10 beans) to get 110 beans (1,100 cedis).
For Year 2 at 10% growth, calculate 10% of the 110 beans (11 beans) and add them to get 121 beans (1,210 cedis). Point out the 11th bean that came from Year 1’s growth!
investigation.safetyNote: Conduct under adult supervision.

investigation.title: Paper-Prototype Usability Test
materials: Two sheets of paper, a pencil, and a classmate who has not seen your drawing.
steps: On Sheet A, draw a cluttered "Version 1" phone screen with 12 tiny buttons and long paragraphs. On Sheet B, draw a clean "Version 2" screen with 3 clear choices.
Show Sheet A to your partner for 5 seconds and ask them how they would book an electrician. Time how long it takes them to find the right button.
Repeat with Sheet B and compare which design was faster, clearer, and needed less explanation.

investigation.title: Cost-Per-Day Civic Maths Check
materials: Exercise book, pencil, and a basic calculator.
steps: Write down the length of a four-year local term in days: 4 × 365 = 1,460 days.
Divide a 50-cedi election handout by 1,460 days (50 ÷ 1,460 ≈ 0.034 cedis, or about 3.4 pesewas per day).
Now compare that 3.4 pesewas per day with the value of clean borehole water and a dry clinic roof serving 5,000 residents every day for 1,460 days.

teacherGuide.overview: An upper-primary and JHS environmental science and citizenship story examining the ecological, health and economic impacts of destructive illegal mining (galamsey) on Ghana’s rivers. It teaches the rigorous scientific distinction between visible turbidity and laboratory-verified chemical contamination, strict child safety around polluted water, and how law enforcement must be paired with sustainable youth livelihoods and land reclamation.
learningGoals: Explain how high turbidity and suspended sediment harm aquatic ecosystems (blocking sunlight for photosynthesis, clogging fish gills, silting riverbeds) and raise water-treatment costs.

Follow strict safety rules: never touch, wade into, or sample polluted water without professional adult supervision and protective equipment.
Explain how environmental protection, lawful governance (EPA Ghana, Water Resources Commission) and sustainable youth employment work together.

investigation.title: Safe Classroom Torch & Turbidity Test
materials: Two clear plastic cups of clean tap water, one teaspoon of clean dry garden soil, a white card, and a small torch (never use polluted river water!).
steps: Leave Cup A filled with clear tap water. Stir one teaspoon of clean garden soil into Cup B to simulate suspended sediment.
Hold the white card behind Cup A and shine the torch through the side — notice how bright the light is on the card.
Shine the torch through Cup B — notice how the suspended soil scatters and blocks the light beam, just as turbid water blocks sunlight from underwater plants.

investigation.title: Airflow Winnowing Separation Test
materials: A tray, 20 dried beans or small pebbles, 20 tiny pieces of dry paper or dry leaf husks, and a piece of stiff card to fan gently.
steps: Mix the 20 dried beans and 20 tiny paper husks together in a small cup.
Pour the mixture slowly from a height of 20 cm onto the tray while a partner waves the stiff card gently from the side to create a light breeze.
Observe where the heavy beans land compared with where the light paper husks blow!

teacherGuide.overview: A rich JHS 1–3 entrepreneurship, food-science and career-technology story showing how Ghanaian agro-processing turns perishable farm gluts into shelf-stable products. learningGoals: Explain how agro-processing (moisture reduction, hygienic packaging) prevents post-harvest loss and adds economic value to Ghanaian crops.

Calculate batch cost, revenue, gross profit and percentage margin (200 + 150 = 350 cedis cost; 100 × 5 = 500 cedis revenue; 500 − 350 = 150 cedis profit = 30% margin).
Recognise that sustainable enterprises require skills, ethical compliance, financing discipline and years of persistence.

investigation.title: Safe Sun-Drying Moisture Loss Observation
materials: One fresh slice of plantain or apple, a small clean plate, a fine mesh cover (to keep flies away), and a kitchen scale (or ruler to measure thickness).
steps: Measure the starting mass (or thickness in millimetres) of a thin slice of fresh plantain on a clean plate covered with clean mesh.
Place the covered plate in warm sunshine for 4 hours, then measure the mass (or thickness) again.
Observe how the slice becomes lighter, firmer and drier as water evaporates — the exact principle behind food dehydration!

teacherGuide.overview: A Primary 6 to JHS 2 history, physics and civic-engineering story set on a fictional school excursion to the Akosombo Dam. Learners trace energy transformations in hydroelectricity, calculate station output, and examine the real historical benefits, human resettlement (80,000 people across 700+ villages) and ecological impacts of the Volta River Project.
learningGoals: Trace the four-stage energy conversion in a hydroelectric station: gravitational potential → kinetic → mechanical → electrical energy.
Explain how spinning magnets inside copper coils induce an electric current (Faraday’s electromagnetic induction).
Calculate total power output across multiple generating units (6 × 170 MW = 1,020 MW).
Evaluate both the national industrial benefits and the human/environmental trade-offs (displacement of ~80,000 people, schistosomiasis, downstream flow changes) of the Volta River Project.

beforeReading: Locate the Volta River, Lake Volta and Akosombo on a map of Ghana and ask learners where the electricity in their community comes from.
Clarify that while Sena, Kwaku and Grandma Akosua are fictional characters, the dates, dimensions and historical facts about the Akosombo Dam are real.
whileReading: Pause at page 4 and page 6 to have learners draw arrows showing how potential energy becomes kinetic, mechanical and electrical energy.
Pause at page 9 to discuss what families lose when ancestral farmlands and villages are flooded, even when new houses are built.
afterReading: Divide the class into four stakeholder groups (industrial planners, resettled farmers, public-health officers, downstream clam fishers) to propose how a modern project should protect everyone affected.
discussion: Why did Ghana’s post-independence leaders view abundant electricity as essential for industrialisation?
Why is hydroelectricity considered a renewable energy source, and why does Ghana today combine hydropower with solar and thermal power?
How does remembering the sacrifice of the 80,000 resettled citizens change the way we think about using electricity responsibly?
reflection: What Would You Build, Discover or Change? If you were designing a clean energy project for your district today, how would you generate power while protecting local families and nature?

mathsExtension.task: Akosombo has 6 generating units rated at 170 MW each. If 5 units are running at full capacity and 1 unit is shut down for scheduled maintenance, how many megawatts are being generated?
Construction of the Akosombo Dam began in 1961 and the dam was inaugurated in 1966. How many years passed between the start of construction and the inauguration?

support: Use the waterwheel investigation and focus on the three words: penstock (pipe), turbine (wheel) and generator (magnet + wire).
stretch: Research how the Kpong Dam and Bui Dam complement Akosombo, including how Bui added floating and land-based solar panels to form a hydro-solar hybrid plant.

culturalNotes: Sena (Ewe), Tetteh (Ga-Dangme), and Kwaku / Akosua (Akan) reflect the diverse Ghanaian communities living around and served by the Volta Basin.
Communities in the Volta Basin hold deep cultural and historical ties to ancestral lands, rivers and sacred groves, making the 1960s resettlement a profound historical sacrifice.
localiseThis: Connect to your region’s electricity supply (NEDCo or ECG) and any nearby solar mini-grids, dams or substations.

whatWeKnow: The Akosombo Dam was constructed between 1961 and 1965 and officially inaugurated in January 1966, creating Lake Volta (~8,502 km² surface area).
Hydroelectric stations convert gravitational potential energy of elevated water into kinetic energy, mechanical turbine rotation, and electrical energy via electromagnetic induction.
Formation of Lake Volta required resettling approximately 80,000 people from over 700 villages into 52 resettlement towns and altered aquatic and downstream ecosystems.
whatWeAreStillDiscovering: Energy engineers are researching how floating solar photovoltaics (floatovoltaics) on reservoirs can generate extra power while reducing water evaporation during hot dry seasons.
Ecologists and hydrologists continue studying how environmental flow releases from dams can best restore downstream river habitats and livelihoods.

investigation.title: Build a Simple Classroom Waterwheel Turbine
materials: A clean plastic bottle cap or small cardboard disc coated in tape
6 small pieces of stiff plastic cut from a yoghurt cup (for blades)
A wooden skewer or pencil (as the shaft)
A plastic jug of water and a bucket to catch the water
steps: Slot or tape the 6 small plastic blades evenly around the rim of the bottle cap to form a miniature turbine wheel, and push the wooden skewer through the centre.
Hold the skewer loosely with two fingers over an empty bucket and pour water steadily from the jug onto the side blades from 10 cm above.
Now pour the water from 30 cm above the wheel and compare how fast the wheel spins.
investigation.whatToNotice: Pouring water from a greater height gives the water more gravitational potential energy, which turns into faster kinetic motion and spins the turbine wheel faster—just like the high water level above the Akosombo penstocks!
investigation.safetyNote: Use blunt scissors under adult supervision and perform the pouring test over a bucket or outdoors so the floor stays dry.

factCheck.claim: Akosombo Dam was built between 1961 and 1965 (inaugurated January 1966), stands 114 m above the riverbed, and has an installed capacity of 1,020 MW across 6 units.
factCheck.explanation: Constructed by Impregilo under the Volta River Authority (established 1961), the rock-fill embankment dam is 114 m high and 671 m long; following the 1999–2006 retrofit, its 6 units are rated at 170 MW each (1,020 MW total).
factCheck.reference: Volta River Authority (VRA) Official Technical Profile of the Akosombo Generating Station.

factCheck.claim: Creating Lake Volta displaced approximately 80,000 people from more than 700 villages into 52 resettlement towns.
factCheck.explanation: The VRA resettlement programme relocated roughly 80,000 residents from over 700 villages flooded by the 8,502 km² reservoir.
factCheck.reference: Chambers, R. (ed.) The Volta Resettlement Experience; Volta River Authority Historical Archives.

reviewerNotes: Confirm first syllable vowel (kway vs kwah).

characters: Mansa: a fourteen-year-old Ghanaian girl in JHS 2 in Techiman, wearing a green-and-cream school uniform, braided hair with green beads, and carrying a tablet computer.
Tariq: Mansa’s fourteen-year-old classmate and drone pilot in the school STEM club, wearing a green-and-cream uniform and spectacles.

teacherGuide.overview: A JHS 1–3 artificial intelligence, computer vision and agricultural entrepreneurship story set in Techiman. Learners discover how machine-learning models learn from training data, why unrepresentative studio datasets fail in real Ghanaian farm conditions, why separate test sets and farmer privacy/consent matter, and why AI must support—never replace—human experts.
learningGoals: Explain how a supervised machine-learning model learns patterns from labelled training data and is evaluated on unseen test data.
Distinguish between a false positive (flagging a healthy dusty leaf as diseased) and a false negative (missing a truly diseased leaf in shadow).
Calculate model accuracy rates from test counts (9/20 = 45% vs 180/200 = 90%).
Explain why data privacy, informed consent and human-in-the-loop oversight are essential in AI engineering.

beforeReading: Ask learners: "How do you recognise the difference between a ripe mango and an unripe mango? How would you teach a computer that has never seen a mango to tell the difference?"
whileReading: Pause at page 5 and calculate the percentage: 9 correct out of 20 plots = (9 ÷ 20) × 100 = 45%.
Pause at page 7 to discuss why flying a camera over farms requires clear privacy rules and neighbour consent.
afterReading: Run the classroom "Paper-Leaf Classifier" game so students experience how a limited training set leads to misclassification.
discussion: Why did a model with 90% accuracy on studio photos fail on Uncle Kwabena’s farm?
What would happen if a farmer sprayed expensive pesticide every time an unverified AI app gave a false positive?
Why did Tariq say testing a model on its own training images is like giving a student the exam questions before the test?
reflection: What Would You Build, Discover or Change? What real problem in your community could a sensor, app or tool help solve, and which human experts would you partner with?

mathsExtension.task: In the first field trial, Mansa’s model tested 20 plots and got 9 right. What percentage was correct, and what percentage was misclassified?
In the second trial, the retrained model was tested on 200 unseen field images and classified 180 correctly. What was its accuracy percentage, and how many images did it still misclassify?
mathsExtension.answer: Accuracy: (180 ÷ 200) × 100 = 90%. Misclassified: 200 − 180 = 20 images (10%), showing why human verification is still needed.

support: Focus on the everyday meaning of "training examples", "false alarm (false positive)" and "missed problem (false negative)".
stretch: Design a simple confusion matrix (2×2 table of Actual Healthy / Actual Diseased vs Predicted Healthy / Predicted Diseased) using the 20 plots from Page 5 (9 correct, 8 false positives, 3 false negatives).

culturalNotes: Techiman in the Bono East Region is one of West Africa’s major agricultural market hubs, bringing together farmers and traders from across Ghana.
localiseThis: Substitute the main crop grown around your school (e.g., cassava mosaic disease, cocoa black pod, millet, or tomato blight).

whatWeKnow: Supervised image-classification models learn statistical patterns from labelled training images and often fail ("domain shift" or dataset bias) when deployed in lighting, soil or weather conditions absent from their training set.
Separating training data from an independent hold-out test set is required to measure how well a model generalises to unseen data.
Agricultural AI tools work best as decision-support systems paired with human agronomists and farmers rather than autonomous chemical-spraying triggers.
whatWeAreStillDiscovering: Computer-vision researchers in Ghana and across Africa are developing lightweight edge-AI models that can run offline on low-cost smartphones without needing mobile internet in remote farms.

investigation.title: Spot Training-Data Bias with a Classroom Sorting Game
materials: 10 index cards or slips of paper with drawings of leaves
Coloured pencils (green, yellow and brown)
steps: Have Group A create 6 "Training Cards": draw 3 healthy green round leaves and 3 diseased yellow pointed leaves. Show ONLY these 6 cards to Group B and ask Group B to write down the rule for spotting a diseased leaf.
Now hand Group B 4 "Real Farm Test Cards" that include a healthy pointed green leaf with a tiny brown soil speck and a round leaf with yellow disease spots.
Check whether Group B’s rule misclassified the pointed healthy leaf or the round diseased leaf, and discuss how adding more varied training cards fixes the rule.
investigation.whatToNotice: When the training cards only showed one leaf shape or lacked soil specks, the rule learned the wrong shortcut—just like Mansa’s first AI model!
investigation.safetyNote: Standard classroom paper activity; no special hazards.

factCheck.claim: Machine-learning image classifiers trained on laboratory leaf images (such as PlantVillage studio photos) often drop sharply in accuracy when tested on real field images unless retrained on diverse field data.
factCheck.explanation: Peer-reviewed agricultural computer-vision studies show models achieving >90% accuracy on uniform-background lab datasets frequently drop below 50% on real field photos due to background clutter, illumination variance and dust.
factCheck.reference: Mohanty et al. (2016), Frontiers in Plant Science; Ferentinos (2018), Computers and Electronics in Agriculture.

characters: Adwoa: an inquisitive ten-year-old Ghanaian girl in Primary 5, wearing a neat yellow-and-brown school pinafore on school days and a bright orange dress on weekends, carrying a notebook.
Papa Kofi: Adwoa’s father, a skilled cocoa farmer in Sefwi Wiawso in his forties, wearing rubber boots and a blue work shirt.
Mama Efua: Adwoa’s mother, a treasurer of the local cocoa farmers’ cooperative, wearing a patterned green-and-gold cloth.
Auntiebaaba / Auntie Baaba: a food scientist and chocolate maker at a Ghanaian chocolate factory in Tema, wearing a white lab coat and hairnet.

narrationPlan.voice: Warm, appreciative Ghanaian English storyteller; lively curiosity for Adwoa and proud expertise for Papa Kofi, Mama Efua and Auntie Baaba.

culturalNotes: Celebrates both Ghanaian cocoa farmers and Ghanaian food scientists adding value locally in Tema and across the country.

teacherGuide.overview: A Primary 4–6 agricultural science, trade and entrepreneurship story following a cocoa bean from a sustainable shaded farm in Sefwi Wiawso to a Ghanaian chocolate factory in Tema. Learners explore fermentation chemistry, post-harvest quality control, cocoa processing (nibs, liquor, butter, powder, conching), child-safe farming standards, and the economics of value addition.
learningGoals: Describe the post-harvest science of cocoa on the farm: 6-day fermentation and 7–10-day sun-drying to under 8% moisture.
Trace factory processing from roasted beans to cocoa nibs, cocoa liquor, cocoa butter, cocoa powder and conched chocolate.
Distinguish gross retail revenue from net profit using an illustrative value-addition cost breakdown.
Explain why sustainable shade-tree agroforestry and strict child-safe farm rules protect Ghana’s cocoa heritage.

beforeReading: Show learners a picture of a cocoa pod and a bar of Ghanaian chocolate (or cocoa powder) and ask: "What steps happen between the tree and the tin?"
Note that the financial numbers on pages 8–9 are illustrative classroom examples designed to teach cost vs profit arithmetic, as real market prices change over time.
whileReading: Pause after page 4 to ask why unfermented cocoa beans do not taste like chocolate even if you roast them.
Pause after page 9 to work through the cost table on the board: 300 cedis (beans) + 700 cedis (other inputs, wages, energy, packaging) = 1,000 cedis total cost.
afterReading: Have learners pick another Ghanaian crop (cassava, shea nuts, mango, groundnuts, tiger nuts) and draw a 4-step "Raw to Value-Added Product" poster.
discussion: Why do shade trees help a cocoa farm stay healthy for many years?
Why is it wrong to assume that the entire price difference between raw cocoa beans and a retail chocolate bar is pure profit?
What new jobs are created in Ghana when cocoa is processed into butter, powder, cosmetics and chocolate bars locally?
reflection: What Would You Build, Discover or Change? Choose one crop grown in your region—what new snack, drink or household product could you make from it, and how would you package it cleanly?

mathsExtension.task: In the illustrative workshop example, 100 chocolate bars sell for 12 cedis each (1,200 cedis total revenue). Raw cocoa beans cost 300 cedis and processing, ingredients, wages and packaging cost 700 cedis. What is the net profit per bar?
mathsExtension.answer: Total profit = 1,200 − (300 + 700) = 200 cedis. Profit per bar = 200 ÷ 100 = 2 cedis per bar.

mathsExtension.task: If a cooperative dries 500 kg of wet fermented beans and loses 55% of the weight as water evaporates during sun-drying, how many kilograms of dry cocoa beans remain?
mathsExtension.answer: Water lost = 55% of 500 = 275 kg. Dry beans remaining = 500 − 275 = 225 kg (45% of 500 kg).

support: Create a simple 5-card picture sequence: Pod → White Beans → Brown Dried Beans → Cocoa Liquor/Butter → Chocolate Bar.
stretch: Investigate how by-products of the cocoa pod (such as cocoa pod husks and mucilage sweatings) are used in Ghana to make potash black soap (alata samina) and fruit juice.

culturalNotes: Since Tetteh Quarshie introduced Amelonado cocoa pods to Akuapem Mampong in 1879, cocoa has been central to Ghanaian rural livelihoods and national pride.
localiseThis: In northern coastal or savannah zones where cocoa does not grow, compare the cocoa value chain with the shea butter (Vitellaria paradoxa) or cashew value chain.

whatWeKnow: Cocoa flowers and pods grow directly on the trunk and older branches (cauliflory) and are pollinated primarily by tiny biting midges (Forcipomyia) that thrive in moist shaded leaf litter.
Microbial fermentation (yeasts, lactic acid bacteria and acetic acid bacteria) over ~6 days and sun-drying to ~7.5% moisture are essential to develop chocolate flavour precursors and prevent mould.
Roasting, winnowing, grinding into cocoa liquor, hydraulic pressing into butter and cake, and conching are the core industrial steps of chocolate manufacturing.
whatWeAreStillDiscovering: Food scientists at the Cocoa Research Institute of Ghana (CRIG) continue researching new value-added products from cocoa pulp, husks and flavanol-rich extracts.

investigation.title: Observe How Fat (Cocoa Butter) and Solids Behave in Warm Water
materials: 1 spoonful of unsweetened cocoa powder
2 cups of warm water and 1 spoonful of cooking oil or shea/cocoa butter
Two clear cups and a spoon
steps: In Cup A, stir a spoonful of cocoa powder into warm water and observe how the fine solid particles suspend in the liquid.
In Cup B, add a small drop of oil or melted shea/cocoa butter to warm water and observe how pure plant fats separate unless mixed and emulsified.
Discuss how pressing cocoa liquor separates the fat (cocoa butter) from the dry solids (cocoa powder).
investigation.whatToNotice: Cocoa beans contain both natural fat (cocoa butter) and dry cocoa solids; separating or recombining them in precise ratios lets food scientists make either drinkable cocoa powder or smooth solid chocolate!
investigation.safetyNote: Use warm tap water (never boiling water) under teacher supervision.

factCheck.claim: Ghanaian cocoa beans undergo ~6 days of heap or tray fermentation followed by sun-drying to ~7.5% moisture before quality grading.
factCheck.explanation: Standard Ghana Cocoa Board (COCOBOD) and CRIG post-harvest protocols specify 6 days of fermentation with turning and 7–10 days of sun-drying to ~7.5% moisture content.
factCheck.reference: Cocoa Research Institute of Ghana (CRIG) Farmers’ Handbook on Cocoa Production.

pronunciation.guidance: Candidate: "ah-JWAH". The "dw" is the hard part for English engines and is probably not a plain "d" + "w".
reviewerNotes: HIGH RISK: the "dw" cluster. Native speaker to demonstrate and approve a rendering.
Confirm the vowel in the first syllable (oh vs aw).

pronunciation.guidance: Candidate: three soft syllables, "eh-FOO-ah". A two-syllable "EH-fwah" is also heard in English speech.
reviewerNotes: Choose between "eh-FOO-ah" (3 syllables) and "EH-fwah" (2) for the narrator voice.
Supply IPA and mark tone if wanted.

teacherGuide.overview: A Primary 2–4 biodiversity, pollination and insect-navigation story set in a school garden near Aburi. Learners discover how butterflies use compound eyes (including ultraviolet vision), antennae and foot taste receptors, distinguish local habitat navigation from long-distance migration, and separate established biology from open neuroscience questions.
learningGoals: Describe how a butterfly uses its compound eyes, antennae, proboscis and feet to find and feed on flowers.
Explain how butterflies pollinate flowers while sipping nectar.
Explain that not all butterfly species migrate long distances; many Ghanaian butterflies navigate locally using sun position, scents and landmarks.
Distinguish what biologists already know about insect senses from what scientists are still discovering about tiny insect brains.

mathsExtension.task: Nhyira and Kojo counted 6 yellow grass butterflies, 4 black-and-yellow swallowtails and 5 white butterflies in 15 minutes. How many butterflies did they count altogether, and how many more yellow grass butterflies than swallowtails did they see?
mathsExtension.answer: Total = 6 + 4 + 5 = 15 butterflies. Difference = 6 − 4 = 2 more yellow grass butterflies than swallowtails.

support: Act out the four butterfly parts with hand gestures: unrolling proboscis (curled finger), antennae (two fingers above head), compound eyes (hands around eyes) and tasting feet (tapping toes).

culturalNotes: Aburi in the Akuapem South Municipality (Eastern Region) is home to the historic Aburi Botanical Gardens, famous for its rich plant and butterfly diversity.

whatWeKnow: Butterflies see colour and ultraviolet light patterns with their compound eyes, detect airborne odours with their antennae, taste host-plant chemicals with receptors on their feet (tarsi), and sip liquid through a coiled proboscis.

Ghana has over 900 recorded butterfly species; unlike the North American monarch’s multi-generational continental migration, most Ghanaian species navigate locally or shift seasonally within West African habitats.
whatWeAreStillDiscovering: Neurobiologists are still investigating the exact neural circuits in the insect central complex that combine sun-compass cues, visual landmarks and odour plumes into spatial memory.

investigation.title: 10-Minute Quiet Pollinator Tally in the Schoolyard
materials: A notebook or sheet of paper ruled into 3 columns (Butterfly / Bee / Other Insect)
A pencil
A flowering bush or garden patch on the school compound
steps: Stand two steps back from a sunny flowering bush so you do not cast a shadow over the flowers or disturb visiting insects.
For 10 minutes, stay quiet and make one tally mark each time a butterfly, bee or other insect lands on a flower.
Add up the tally marks in each column and compare which flower colour received the most visits.
investigation.whatToNotice: Staying still and quiet lets pollinators behave naturally, and different insects often prefer different flower shapes and colours!
investigation.safetyNote: Never touch, swat at or trap bees, wasps or butterflies; learners with insect-sting allergies should observe from a safe paved walkway with the teacher.

factCheck.claim: Ghana has over 900 butterfly species, and citrus swallowtails (Papilio demodocus) are common across Ghanaian gardens and farms.
factCheck.explanation: Torben Larsen’s Butterflies of West Africa documents over 900 butterfly species in Ghana, with Papilio demodocus widespread wherever citrus and garden flowers grow.
factCheck.reference: Larsen, T. B. (2005). Butterflies of West Africa; Ghana Wildlife Society.

teacherGuide.overview: A Primary 6 to JHS 2 financial-literacy and mathematics story set in Ho. Learners work through exact Ghana cedi calculations comparing simple and compound interest over 3 years (1,000 → 1,100 → 1,210 → 1,331 cedis), understand inflation and debt compounding, and learn how to spot unlicensed get-rich-quick Ponzi scams.
learningGoals: Calculate multi-year simple interest and compound interest in Ghana cedis and explain why compounding grows faster over time.
Explain how inflation reduces the purchasing power of idle cash.
Explain that compounding also applies to unpaid debt, making high-interest loans grow rapidly.
Identify warning signs of financial fraud (unusually high "guaranteed" returns, pressure to act fast, lack of Bank of Ghana or SEC Ghana licensing).

beforeReading: Ask learners: "If someone offered you 1,000 cedis plus 100 cedis every year (simple), or 1,000 cedis growing by 10% of the new total each year (compound), which would be bigger after 3 years?"
whileReading: Have every learner write down the Year 1 (1,100), Year 2 (1,210) and Year 3 (1,331) calculations in their own notebook alongside Afia on pages 4–6.
Pause at page 8 to discuss why scammers use urgency ("today only!") and greed ("double in 7 days!") to trick people.
afterReading: Compare the 3-year table of Simple vs Compound interest on the chalkboard and compute Year 4 together (1,331 + 133.10 = 1,464.10 cedis).
discussion: Why is keeping all long-term savings in a box at home risky both physically and economically (inflation)?
How does compound interest hurt a borrower who takes a high-interest loan and misses payments?
What two Ghanaian regulatory bodies license banks and investment firms? (Bank of Ghana and the Securities and Exchange Commission — SEC Ghana.)
reflection: What Would You Build, Discover or Change? What is one educational or enterprise goal you want to save for over the next three years, and what rule will protect your family from financial scams?

mathsExtension.task: Calculate the difference after 3 years between 1,000 cedis at 10% simple interest per year and 1,000 cedis at 10% annual compound interest.
mathsExtension.answer: Simple interest after 3 years: 1,000 + (3 × 100) = 1,300 cedis. Compound interest after 3 years: 1,331 cedis. Difference: 1,331 − 1,300 = 31 cedis.

mathsExtension.task: Continue Afia’s 10% compound interest table for one more year (Year 4), starting from the Year 3 balance of 1,331 cedis.

support: Use counters or paper strips of 100 cedis to model Year 1 (10 strips + 1 strip = 11 strips) and Year 2 (11 strips + 1.1 strips = 12.1 strips).
stretch: Calculate what happens if someone borrows 1,000 cedis from an unlicensed lender charging 20% compound interest per month and makes no payments for 2 months (Month 1: 1,200 cedis; Month 2: 1,200 + 240 = 1,440 cedis).

culturalNotes: Ho is the capital of the Volta Region; Yao (Ewe for a boy born on Thursday) and Afia / Akua (Akan day names for Friday / Wednesday) reflect everyday Ghanaian family life.
localiseThis: Point out regulated rural and community banks, credit unions, and Bank of Ghana / SEC Ghana public advisories in your area.

whatWeKnow: Compound growth follows the mathematical formula A = P(1 + r)^n, where interest earned in each period is added to the principal for the next period.
Inflation erodes the real purchasing power of uninvested cash whenever the inflation rate exceeds 0%.
Under Ghanaian law, deposit-taking institutions are regulated by the Bank of Ghana (BoG) and capital-market investment schemes by the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) Ghana.
whatWeAreStillDiscovering: Behavioural economists continue researching how youth financial-literacy education and visual compounding tools improve long-term household savings habits.

investigation.title: Build a Visual Staircase of Simple vs Compound Growth
materials: A sheet of squared (grid) paper
Two coloured pencils (blue for Simple Interest, green for Compound Interest)
A ruler
steps: Let 1 grid square equal 10 cedis (so 1,000 cedis = 100 squares, or draw bars to scale where 1 cm = 100 cedis).
Draw pairs of bars for Year 0 (1,000 vs 1,000), Year 1 (1,100 vs 1,100), Year 2 (1,200 vs 1,210), Year 3 (1,300 vs 1,331) and Year 4 (1,400 vs 1,464.10).
Shade the extra "interest-on-interest" top section of each green Compound bar and notice how that shaded section grows wider every year.
investigation.whatToNotice: In Year 1 the two bars are equal, but in every year after Year 1 the compound bar pulls further ahead because each year’s interest starts earning its own interest!
investigation.safetyNote: Standard classroom graphing activity; no special safety hazards.

factCheck.claim: 1,000 cedis compounded annually at 10% grows to 1,100 cedis in Year 1, 1,210 cedis in Year 2, and 1,331 cedis in Year 3.
factCheck.reference: Standard compound-interest mathematics: A = P(1 + r)^n.

factCheck.claim: Unusually high "guaranteed" short-term investment returns are a primary red flag of Ponzi and financial fraud schemes.
factCheck.explanation: Both the Bank of Ghana and the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) Ghana warn citizens that legitimate investments carry risk and that schemes promising guaranteed rapid doubling of money are fraudulent.
factCheck.reference: Bank of Ghana & SEC Ghana Public Investor Protection Advisories.

teacherGuide.overview: A Primary 5 to JHS 1 science, civic-leadership and values story set in the fictional village of Nsuom. Learners see how faith in God inspires unity, diligence and service alongside scientific hydrogeology, strict water-safety rules (why classroom filters never make water drinkable), laboratory testing, transparent public budgeting and preventive maintenance.
learningGoals: Explain why a simple sand-and-cloth filter only removes visible sediment and NEVER removes microscopic pathogens or dissolved chemicals.
Describe how groundwater is stored in underground aquifers and why boreholes must be sited uphill from latrines, sealed and laboratory-tested.
Calculate multi-step community project budgets (200 households × 15 cedis × 12 months = 36,000 cedis + 64,000 grant = 100,000 cedis).
Explain how faith-inspired values, interfaith unity, scientific expertise and transparent public accounting work together to solve community problems.

Why did Engineer Asante refuse to let anyone drink the clear borehole water until the laboratory certificate arrived?
Why did the old hand-pump stay broken for six months, and how did the new 500-cedi monthly maintenance fund prevent that mistake from happening again?

mathsExtension.task: Nsuom puts 500 cedis per month into a bank maintenance account. After 24 months (2 years), how much has been saved, and if a replacement solar pump controller costs 4,200 cedis, how much remains in the maintenance fund after paying for the repair?
mathsExtension.answer: Saved in 24 months: 500 × 24 = 12,000 cedis. Remaining after repair: 12,000 − 4,200 = 7,800 cedis.

mathsExtension.task: In the 100,000-cedi borehole project, the grant covered 64,000 cedis and the community raised 36,000 cedis. What percentage of the total cost did the community raise?

support: Draw the underground cross-section showing rain soaking into soil → porous rock aquifer → sealed borehole pipe → storage tank → tap.

culturalNotes: In Ghanaian towns and villages, Water and Sanitation Management Teams (WSMTs) work with traditional authorities, Assembly Members and diverse religious communities to manage rural water systems.

whatWeKnow: Simple mechanical filtration through gravel, sand and cloth removes suspended turbidity (sediment) but does NOT remove dissolved chemicals or microscopic pathogens (bacteria, viruses, protozoa).

Safe rural drinking-water engineering requires hydrogeological siting, sanitary borehole sealing, accredited laboratory testing (microbiological and physicochemical under GSA GS 175 / WHO guidelines) and residual disinfection.
Dedicated community maintenance funds and trained local technicians dramatically reduce rural borehole downtime.
whatWeAreStillDiscovering: Hydrogeologists in Ghana use satellite remote sensing and geophysical mapping to chart deep Basement Complex fracture aquifers resilient to multi-year droughts.

investigation.title: See Why Sediment Filtration Is Only Step One (Non-Drinkable Demo)
materials: A clear plastic bottle with the bottom cut off by the teacher
Clean pebbles, coarse sand, fine sand and a piece of clean cotton cloth
A jar of muddy water mixed with a drop of safe food colouring (to represent dissolved substances)
steps: Have the teacher secure the cloth over the bottle neck and layer pebbles, coarse sand and fine sand inside to model how soil layers trap large dirt particles.
Pour the muddy coloured water through the sand layers into a clear cup below.
Observe that while the brown mud particles are trapped by the sand, the food colouring (and any invisible microbes) passes right through into the cup!
investigation.whatToNotice: The coloured water in the bottom cup proves that even when big mud particles are filtered out, dissolved substances and microscopic germs pass straight through—which is why classroom-filtered water must NEVER be drunk!
investigation.safetyNote: STRICT SAFETY RULE: Label the cup "DO NOT DRINK — SCIENCE DEMO ONLY" and pour the water on outdoor plants after the demonstration; wash hands with soap and safe running water.

factCheck.claim: A simple sand-and-cloth filter removes suspended sediment but does not make water microbiologically or chemically safe to drink.
factCheck.explanation: Pore spaces in simple sand and cloth filters (typically >10–50 micrometres) are far larger than bacteria (~0.5–5 micrometres), viruses (~0.02–0.3 micrometres) and dissolved ions (fluoride, arsenic, nitrates), requiring disinfection and laboratory verification.
factCheck.reference: World Health Organization (WHO) Guidelines for Drinking-water Quality; Ghana Standards Authority GS 175.

reviewerNotes: Confirm final vowel (meh vs mee) and the "kw" onset.

investigation.title: Supervised Classroom Sand-and-Water Tray Demonstration
materials: A shallow plastic or metal tray
Clean sand or soil
A small cup of water
steps: Shape clean sand at one end of the shallow tray to model a gentle beach slope.
Pour water carefully into the other end of the tray.
Gently tilt or wave a ruler in the water and observe how grains of sand shift and move.
investigation.whatToNotice: Moving water picks up and transports sand grains (sediment), changing the shape of the model shoreline.

factCheck.claim: Waves, currents, storms and changes in sea level can affect coastlines, and local conditions must be investigated.
factCheck.explanation: Coastal morphodynamics depend on wave energy, longshore currents, sediment supply, human activities and relative sea-level change.

mathsExtension.task: Four baskets cost GH₵15 each (GH₵60 total) and a customer pays GH₵100 (GH₵40 change). If Auntie Serwaa paid GH₵44 to buy and transport those four baskets, what is her actual profit?
mathsExtension.answer: GH₵60 sales revenue - GH₵44 expenses = GH₵16 profit.

investigation.title: Classroom Market Record-Book Design
materials: Ruled exercise paper
Ruler and pencils
steps: Draw three clear columns labelled "Item", "Money In (Sales)" and "Money Out (Expenses)".
Record the story’s sale of 4 baskets of oranges at GH₵15 each (GH₵60).
Subtract an example supplier and transport expense of GH₵44 to find the remaining profit (GH₵16).
investigation.whatToNotice: Keeping clear written records prevents confusion and shows the true difference between total sales and net profit.

teacherGuide.overview: Do not collect or breed live mosquitoes for classroom activities. Use photographs, diagrams and supervised environmental observations. learningGoals: Distinguish between the organism that causes malaria (Plasmodium parasite) and the vector that transmits it (infected female Anopheles mosquito).

Why is it important never to self-diagnose or take medicine without a health professional’s advice?

mathsExtension.task: If a community clinic tests 40 patients who have a fever and 25 test positive for malaria while 15 have other causes of fever, what fraction of the fever patients did NOT have malaria?
mathsExtension.answer: 15 out of 40 patients (or 3/8), showing why testing is essential before treatment.

support: Draw a simple 3-box chain on the board: Plasmodium parasite → Infected female Anopheles mosquito → Transmission to human.

whatWeKnow: Human malaria is caused by Plasmodium parasites transmitted through the bites of infected female Anopheles mosquitoes.
Insecticide-treated bed nets, vector management and prompt professional testing and treatment reduce malaria illness.
whatWeAreStillDiscovering: Scientists continue researching more effective malaria vaccines, new antimalarial medicines and ways to overcome insecticide resistance.

investigation.title: Paper Model of the Mosquito Life Cycle & Prevention Poster

Coloured pencils or markers
Published reference diagrams of the mosquito life cycle

investigation.whatToNotice: Interrupting breeding sites and using treated bed nets reduce bites, while clinic testing ensures accurate diagnosis.
investigation.safetyNote: Do NOT collect, keep or breed live mosquitoes or larvae, and do not touch stagnant water.

teacherGuide.overview: Teach the difference between observation, hypothesis, evidence and unanswered questions. Use supervised night-sky observation where practical. Never point telescopes or binoculars at the Sun without appropriate certified solar equipment and expert supervision.
learningGoals: Explain why looking at distant stars is looking back in time because light takes time to travel.

Distinguish between established astronomical evidence (thousands of known exoplanets, gravitational observations in galaxies, cosmic expansion) and open questions (the particle nature of dark matter, dark energy, and whether life exists beyond Earth).
Apply media literacy by checking sources and requiring credible evidence before accepting sensational claims.

beforeReading: Ask learners what they have noticed when looking up at the night sky on a clear evening and what questions they have wondered about.
whileReading: Pause at Page 3 for the quick question on why scientists investigate dark matter.
On Page 5 and Page 6, discuss why checking sources matters and why "We do not know yet" is an honest and exciting scientific answer.
afterReading: Complete the five end-of-story activities covering light travel time, whether life beyond Earth is confirmed, dark matter, media literacy, and open scientific questions.
discussion: What did Araba mean when she wrote, "Evidence can reveal a mystery without solving every part of it"?
Why is it important to separate an exciting possibility (like life on another planet) from confirmed evidence?
reflection: What is one scientific question about the universe or nature that you would love to help investigate one day?

mathsExtension.task: If light from a bright star takes 25 years to reach Earth, how old was the light we see tonight when it left that star?
mathsExtension.answer: 25 years old — we see the star as it was 25 years ago.

support: Create a two-column chart on the board titled "What Scientists Have Confirmed" and "Questions Scientists Are Still Investigating".
stretch: Have learners take a sensational science headline and write three questions they would ask to verify whether the source and evidence are credible.

culturalNotes: Ghana hosts the Ghana Radio Astronomy Observatory at Kuntunse, inspiring young Ghanaian astronomers and engineers.
localiseThis: Encourage learners to observe the night sky from a safe courtyard or veranda with a parent or guardian and sketch the brightest stars or the Moon’s phase.

whatWeKnow: Light travels at a finite speed, so light from distant stars takes years to reach Earth.
Astronomers have confirmed thousands of exoplanets orbiting other stars (including some in binary star systems) and strong evidence for cosmic expansion.
whatWeAreStillDiscovering: No confirmed direct detection has yet established the particle nature of dark matter, the nature of dark energy remains an open question, and life beyond Earth has not been confirmed.

investigation.title: Supervised Night-Sky Observation & Evidence vs. Mystery Chart
materials: Notebook and pencil
Printed star chart (optional)
steps: With a parent or guardian at home in the evening, step into a safe courtyard and observe the night sky for 10 minutes with the naked eye.
Record three things you can directly observe (e.g., Moon phase, differences in star brightness or colour).
Write down two questions that cannot be answered by naked-eye observation alone and explain what tools or evidence scientists would need.
investigation.whatToNotice: Direct observation is the starting point of astronomy, while careful measurement and evidence separate confirmed facts from open mysteries.
investigation.safetyNote: CRITICAL SAFETY RULE: Never look at the Sun directly and NEVER point telescopes, binoculars or cameras at the Sun without certified solar filters and expert supervision—doing so causes immediate, permanent blindness.

factCheck.claim: Thousands of exoplanets have been discovered; dark matter is inferred from gravitational observations without confirmed direct particle detection; life beyond Earth is unconfirmed.
factCheck.explanation: NASA’s Exoplanet Archive lists over 5,500 confirmed exoplanets (including circumbinary planets such as Kepler-16b); dark matter and dark energy remain active areas of cosmological research.
factCheck.reference: NASA Exoplanet Archive; International Astronomical Union (IAU); European Space Agency (ESA) Cosmology briefings
